This study investigates the generalization performance of two-layer neural networks for calculating the ground state of a $d$-dimensional hypercube governed by the Schrödinger equation. Under the premise that the ground state can be found within a specific type of space called the spectral Barron space, this research demonstrates that the two-layer neural network is capable of approximately calculating the ground state with a high probability by training it using a sufficiently large number of i.i.d. random samples. Furthermore, it has been established that the ground states of several universal models, including the Gaussian free field and the discrete $\Delta+\beta$-$\mathbb{Z}^d$ Ising model, can be found within the spectral Barron space. From a statistical viewpoint, this research reveals that the two-layer neural network is capable of consistently estimating the ground state when training on a set of i.i.d. random samples and that its estimation error is limited by a measure of the complexity of the spectral Barron space. Additionally, neural networks trained on these discrete models have been shown to converge uniformly towards the ground state of their Gaussian limit, indicating that the two-layer neural networks are capable of consistently estimating the ground state of the Gaussian free field and the discrete $\Delta+\beta$-$\mathbb{Z}^d$ Ising model. Relevant experimental studies have also been conducted to verify the effectiveness of this research and obtain a better understanding of the two-layer neural networks. Lastly, this research has been extended to investigate the generalization performance of three-layer and $L$-layer neural networks for calculating the ground state of a $d$-dimensional hypercube governed by the Schrödinger equation. Elegans' behavioral and structural biology, scientists can model its brain using available data. A team developed a simulated model of C. Elegans' brain using a state-space representation, which accounted for 285 neurons and incorporated sensory input. This model was trained using data obtained from the.ucemptlab dataset and then compiled to run on a reconfigurable logic circuit in FPGA, for use in robots to facilitate learning and control mechanisms in artificial central nervous systems. Additionally, the model showed compatibility with human brain simulation models, such as the Blue Brain Project, based on its similar state-space representation structure. To further explore its applications, the model was applied to control a robot's navigation of a maze, demonstrating its potential usefulness. Lastly, discussing the possibilities of using this model in the development of hybrid AI systems, in which digital agents collaborate with biological CNS, was also considered. These advancements could ultimately contribute to the evolution of novel technologies in artificial intelligence. In the era of artificial intelligence, computational advancements in text analysis are crucial. Multiple systems have been created to process text across languages; however, existing frameworks still fall short in text comprehension. We propose an innovative text representation framework inspired by human memory, acknowledging that prior approaches often overlooked the inherent complexities of human recollection. We integrated sequential and hierarchical structures, crucial components of human memory, into our method and evaluated its effectiveness using datasets in machine reading and question answering. Although not surpassing state-of-the-art performance in these tasks, our framework has potential as a unified solution for various text analysis problems, including text classification, summarization, translation, and generation. We are confident that our framework can be adapted or extended to other problems, such as text mining, risk analysis, and decision support, due to its versatility. Additionally, we suggest the use of pre-training, a common optimization technique, to enhance the performance of our framework in specific applications. In experimental evaluations, our framework demonstrated the ability to reproduce information from incomplete or distorted text, mimic the capabilities of Transformer-based models, and fill gaps in knowledge from contextual information. Furthermore, our results suggest that our model can mitigate the unintended biases present in datasets, ensuring more reliable processing of text for safety-critical applications. We are confident that our framework addresses a critical need in text analysis and provides a foundation for further research in this domain. The code for our framework is available online. We conducted a study to evaluate how effectively human beings recall information from text and observed a remarkable capacity for memory, exceeding expectations. This finding prompted us to explore whether current AI systems possess similar abilities and identify significant gaps between human capabilities and current AI systems. In particular, we noticed that existing AI systems, including advanced models like Transformers, struggle to comprehend hierarchical structures in text, an essential component of human memory. This distinction prompted us to create a novel text representation framework, incorporating features of human memory, and assess its efficacy using reading and question-answering datasets. Although our model did not surpass current benchmarks; however, we believe it has potential as a unified solution for diverse text analysis tasks and a foundation for future research. In experimental evaluations, our model demonstrated the ability to reproduce information from incomplete or distorted text, contextual information, and mitigate biases in datasets, ensuring more trustworthy processing of text for critical applications. A previous semantics of GP 2 is incomplete because its loop and branching commands utilize big-step operations.  This paper presents an accurate small-step operational semantics for GP 2, effectively capturing the nature of divergent computations.  Achieving small-step definitions for all GP 2 commands requires integrating a host graph stack and associated operations into the transition relation.  It has been shown that this new semantics does not block computations and satisfies the finite nondeterminism property.  It has also been found that GP 2's old semantics fails to satisfy the finite nondeterminism property.  In addition, a comparison with a similar graph language, G#, is made.  In particular, it has been observed that G#'s old semantics also employs big-step operations for loop and branching commands and lacks explicit stack operations.  In contrast to GP 2's new semantics, G#'s transition relation does not contain explicit stack operations either, likely due to system functional nature. To further understand this phenomenon, we introduced a modified model of photoevaporation that is driven by both ultraviolet and X-ray energy from the star, in addition to the previous hydrogen photoevaporation model. The results show that this model provides a superior fit to the observed data, particularly the nuster spectra, and helps to reproduce the soft thermal X-ray emissions accurately. Notably, to achieve these new solutions, we introduce a novel polynomial variant derived from the second kind of Chebyshev polynomials, termed U$_n^(s)$. Further investigation reveals that certain properties unique to Chebyshev polynomials of kinds s and t do not generalize to U$_n^(s)$. Nonetheless, we establish an exact relation between minimal polynomials of third and fourth kinds with negative indices, providing a novel definition for the first kind of Chebyshev polynomials, U$_n^(s)$. Ultimately, this research yields over 180 new factorizations, along with classifications of third and fourth kinds of binary quadratic forms with relatively prime coefficients. Specifically, we find that such forms can be classified using the Rabinowitz invariant for forms with odd forms when the discriminant is negative, and using the Pell-Lambert number for forms with even forms in both cases when the discriminant is positive. Notably, these classifications tie back to the number field sieve factorization method. We also establish that minimal polynomials of third and fourth kinds with negative indices cannot be expressed as factorizations of binary quadratic forms. A final result provides an extension to Weil's theorem on representability by polynomial variants of binary quadratic forms. Ultimately, we find that such binary quadratic forms can be represented by polynomial variants of either the second or first kinds of Chebyshev polynomials, with the first kind represented through a novel definition U$_n^(s)$. Notably, we derive existing results from this generalization, with the first kind represented through $\sqrt{2}$.

The outer points where these branches meet are fixed while rotating. The inner point is capable of moving in two ways, with rotational movement influenced by both elasticity and friction. A detailed analysis in a Hilbert space reveals how the spectrum's asymptotic distribution and structure evolve. It demonstrates that specific eigenvector characteristics form a complete and orthonormal basis. Consequently, we derive the exponential stability of the associated solutions directly from the spectral stability of a corresponding linear system. In particular, we can demonstrate that frictional forces corresponding to friction coefficients as low as $m_2\geq 2^{-3/4}$ are sufficient to prevent instability. Predictions for nuclear masses are achieved through Bayesian neural networks by first understanding the mass surface of even-even nuclei and then considering the relationship between these nuclei and their neighboring nuclei in terms of correlation energies. By integrating known physics into various advanced mass models, a new Bayesian machine learning mass model is developed, demonstrating high accuracy with an estimated uncertainty of about 100 keV. Interestingly, incorporating a dense network architecture led to unexpected geographical separation among advanced mass models, revealing a need to balance model complexity with predictive capabilities. Additionally, a new Bayesian neural network approach to calculating discrete nuclear levels is developed, showing potential for a broad range of applications in nuclear structure spectroscopy. This method integrates known energy correlations of even-even nuclei and their neighboring nuclei in terms of pair blocking and alignment. It then employs Bayesian neural networks to predict unknown energy levels. By comparing experimental energy levels with predicted ones from multiple advanced mass models, a substantial amount of structural information was gathered, particularly for complex regions of nuclear structure such as rare earth, proton-rich, and neutron-rich regions. This method showed high accuracy with an estimated uncertainty of about 200 keV, demonstrating great promise in terms of understanding the complex and intricate structure of nuclei at the extremes of stable and unstable nuclear phases. This work highlights the effectiveness of Bayesian machine learning in understanding nuclear physics and motivating further research into this area. References available upon request. A moving dielectric medium can alter the path of light traveling through it, a phenomenon termed the Fresnel-Fizeau optical drag effect. The induced deviation in the path is directly proportional to the velocity of the medium. Our investigation documents a previously unreported instance of the optical drag effect where the path deviation remains proportional to the medium's velocity but is oriented in a direction counter to the medium's motion. To observe this anomalous effect, we conducted an optical drag experiment under the conditions of electromagnetic transparency and monitored the shift from typical optical drag to zero drag and ultimately the anomalous effect through adjustments to two-photon detuning. The optical drag effect observed under certain two-photon detunings aligns with theoretical predictions outlining a relationship between drag and velocity. Furthermore, we have developed a theoretical explanation for the optical drag effect based on specific detunings and identified conditions for obtaining and manipulating the anomalous effect observed in our study. Our findings have significant implications for the creation of optical drag devices, the advancement of optical communication technologies, and optical sensing tools that can measure medium velocities. Additionally, we have outlined a method for preparing customized optical drag effects and discuss possible applications for fundamental optical research, optical metrology, and quantum information science. Our study serves as a foundational platform for future research into optical drag effects, a phenomenon deemed rare and understudied. Our data collection efficiency was enhanced by the use of superconducting single photon sources, a development offering potential gains in future studies of optical drag effects. Our research provides insights into the general principles governing optical drag effects in light interactions and could have a meaningful impact in fields beyond the context of our current investigation, such as in the creation of optical drag waves, optical resonators, solitons, and soliton lenses. Our data reveals a correlation between optical drag effects and quantum coherence that may be exploited to measure medium velocities. Our research explores the boundaries of optical drag effects, a phenomenon exclusively observed in the quantum regime, to gather fundamental insights and enable novel applications in optical research, metrology, and quantum information science. Our work is singular in its focus on understanding optical drag effects not just as a tool, but also as a means to explore novel phenomena at a fundamental level. Our research has enabled the efficient generation of optical drag effects, a development with substantial implications to advance future studies of optical drag effects and increase data collection efficiency. Our research provides an exclusive platform to study a particular aspect of light interactions, the Fresnel-Fizeau effect, through the manipulation of quantum properties and electromagnetic interactions.

This paper introduces an exact calculation method for worst-case scenario parameter realization in robust optimization problems involving uncertain binary or categorical data. Existing exact algorithms for these problems are computationally resource-intensive, partly due to their increased complexity following reformulation of the problem, and partly due to unknown bounds for decision-independent variables. In contrast, we suggest a Lagrangian dual approach that avoids these issues, which can be easily integrated into existing algorithms. This method is particularly novel because it is tailored to problems with decision-dependent uncertainty, which cannot be easily addressed through other reformulation techniques. We demonstrate that this approach is dual convex and tightly estimates the worst-case scenario for binary and categorical uncertainty cases. Furthermore, we develop a simplified algorithm that achieves convergence to the optimal dual estimate, calculated in each iteration. We also introduce a binary uncertainty example to showcase that the proposed method converges to the exact optimal value when it differs from its dual estimate. This method may also converge to the exact optimal value in cases of non-convex problems, albeit in a sub-linear time complexity relative to the existing algorithms. We further advocate for the use of Bierman's inequality to tighten the lower dual estimate, providing a better starting point for the algorithm with an improved estimation. This proposed method is demonstrated to be dual feasible, achieving a lower dual estimate that in some cases is tighter than the one obtained via the Bierman's inequality alone. Ultimately, we test the proposed method in a non-convex robust optimization problem with binary uncertainty and observe that it yields better results with reduced computational effort compared to the existing algorithms. The understanding of socioeconomic standing has evolved significantly with the accessibility of comprehensive digital records that include real estate information, local attraction data, traffic dynamics, and social media patterns such as online micro-blogging. This research outlines a multidimensional, diverse dataset referred to as "H4M". This dataset consists of data related to four distinct aspects: real estate, local landmarks, traffic behavior, and social media sentiment patterns in Beijing. Due to its complex nature, the H4M dataset challenges researchers with its diverse sources of data. We have developed this dataset to address research questions surrounding the intersection of geographic information systems and social network analysis, as well as to support research in this field. The H4M dataset can also be applied in various fields such as transportation planning, urban mobility systems, commercial real estate assessment, and human behavior studies in Beijing.

The development of pattern extraction algorithms helps gain valuable insights into large datasets by identifying recurring elements and their distributions. However, examining vast amounts of data, including both extracted patterns and results from algorithms, proves challenging and hinders researchers from fully leveraging available analytical tools. To address this issue, we present a novel web-based platform, ApMaP, designed to facilitate in-depth data analysis and understanding by enhancing visualization and management capabilities. Our platform allows users to define custom queries and incorporate results into visualizations, while also providing features to group and compare data. As demonstrated by our analysis of both artificial and real-world datasets, this approach leads to significant discoveries, such as uncovering distinct classes within a seemingly uniform pattern distribution. Problems of control systems design, estimation, and inference can be redefined as optimization problems that require solving continuous-time dynamic equations with constraints. When analytical solutions are not feasible, alternative methods such as numerical discretization or other approximations must be employed. We re-examine specific types of these problems that are associated with difficulties in path-wise analysis, and propose a general framework for addressing them in both deterministic and stochastic contexts. This framework can be applied to problems involving linear or nonlinear systems, and their combinations, facilitating a rigorous mathematical understanding via variational analysis and the exploitation of problem-specific symmetries. We illustrate the proposed framework with several examples of control engineering and data science significance. Furthermore, we leverage the properties of these problems to develop new and advanced techniques, such as cutting-plane methods tailored to dynamic systems, conditional gradient algorithms for continuous-time settings, and other first-order optimization techniques. We confirm the potential of these methods through numerical simulations with real-world data, highlighting their value in practical applications. In 2002, Ted Chen and Robert Ghrist created a simplified version of the first homology group, known as the rigidity group, to measure a topological space's rigidity levels. This space's level of rigidity is determined by the number of certain group configurations present in it. We developed a method to calculate the rigidity group for a torus that has been folded into a cube using the mapping class group's operations. By considering different configurations, we found and proved the torus's rigidity group to have an infinite sequence of generators. We also found the torsion generators' orders to be equal to specific divisors of the torus's surface area. Additionally, we created a method for comparing and combining different rigidity configurations in the mapping class group. This allowed us to discover new relationships between the different types of torus folds. Furthermore, we validated the results from the mapping class group by calculating the first homology group for the universal cover of the torus using a different algebraic approach, thereby verifying the presence of the aforementioned torsion generators' orders. We also applied the same approach to calculate the rigidity group for the surface of three-dimensional spaces, such as the sphere, projective plane, and certain smooth structures on the sphere. While the results for the sphere were previously known, those for the projective plane were newly derived. We failed to determine whether the torsion generators' orders could divide the surface area without a division by five. We were, however, able to confirm the presence of a certain standard configuration in the projective plane's rigidity group. By interpreting the projective plane's different smooth structures as a topological fibration in five, we also obtained new relationships between its mapping class group and universal cover. We made the software used to calculate and derive the results publicly available on the GitHub platform under specific repository names. In the process of our work, we re-identified certain mathematical concepts to ensure consistency with established definitions in the field, especially those related to the projective plane's different smooth structures and certain class group operations. We defined and provided the general definitions for certain mathematical concepts related to the sphere's different topological properties. In our work, we discovered new connections between the different types of torus folds and certain mathematical concepts related to the projective plane. In addition to our new results, our approach also yielded new proofs for certain existing theorems in the field, specifically those related to the projective plane's different smooth structures and certain mathematical concepts related to the sphere.

Our team is currently working on optimizing the design of wide-field X-ray telescopes with particular emphasis on reducing the number of mechanical components including mirrors. By assuming the use of Wolter-I optics, we have developed an innovative approach for determining the mirror prescriptions effectively using simulation tools. These simulations involve modeling deviations from an ideal Wolter-I shape as perturbations, translating these distortions into changes in mirror prescriptions, and assessing the impact of these deviations on telescope performance. Initially, we tested this approach by analyzing the effects of tilt, curvature, and aberrations in mirror surfaces. Next, we incorporated these distortions into a genetic algorithm in order to obtain near-optimal solutions for a specific wide-field X-ray telescope, allowing it to operate efficiently within its structural limitations. Furthermore, we used this technique to investigate various parameters including modification strategies for the spherical surface, consideration of tilt adjustments, influence of aberrations, effects of closed surfaces, and impacts of realistic fabrication inaccuracies. Ultimately, we obtained several solutions which we were able to compare to a classic, conventional design using Monte Carlo simulations, in order to assess their differences in terms of overall efficiency and on-axis resolution. Additionally, we used these simulations to calculate the effects of distortions in the mirror surfaces on a X-ray telescope's performance, allowing for direct comparison of different designs. By analyzing the results, our team identified several interesting trends that could inform the development of future X-ray telescopes. Specifically, we found that modifications to the Wolter-I paraboloid, Wolter-II, and elliptical mirrors effectively reduced the effects of on-axis curvature, sky-singularity, and spherical aberrations. Consequently, this effectively reduced the impacts of spherical aberrations, increased the effective area of the detector, and improved the overall on-axis resolution of the X-ray telescope. Our team is currently working on integrating this new technique with different search algorithms in order to further refine this design optimization method. In particular, we plan to explore the potential benefits of using evolutionary strategies, differential evolution, and Bayesian optimization to guide this design optimization process. By analyzing the results, our team believes that this approach has the potential to inspire improvements not only in X-ray optics, but also in optical systems more broadly. Specifically, our team believes that this technique could effectively reduce the effects of aberrations in optical systems by translating complex distortions into changes in lens prescriptions. By appealing to this analogy, our team believes that this approach has the potential to inspire similar trends in not only X-ray optics, but also in optical systems more broadly.

Researchers frequently apply synthetic control techniques to determine the effect of treatment on a single treated entity within data sets that span multiple periods. The goal of synthetic control is to create a weighted average of units without treatment that mimics the treated entity's pre-intervention outcome trajectory. Initially, the weights used in synthetic control calculations are derived from pre-intervention data and do not consider post-treatment dynamics. This research argues that since the treated entity's post-treatment dynamics often differ from those of the control group, ignoring post-treatment data leads to biased treatment impact estimates. To resolve this challenge, we suggest updating the weights used in synthetic control by optimization methods that incorporate a distance metric. The proposed method enables the creation of a targeted control group that closely matches the treated entity's outcomes across various dimensions, leveraging all available panel data. The technical requirements for consistent estimation are also provided and it is demonstrated that the convergence rate achieved is the fastest possible. Finally, our results from simulated data sets illustrate the advantages of our fully efficient synthetic control method over traditional approaches. The results further suggest that in the relevant practical scenario where the treated entity and control units largely share pre-intervention outcomes, the fully efficient synthetic control method offers an improved alternative to missing match methods. Additional numerical analysis examines the impact of treatment on target entities within the Context Matters Dataset and the MDG Health Dataset, and reveals the fully efficient synthetic control method to be particularly effective when a variety of post-treatment outcomes can be accurately matched. By contrast, we found that in the scenario of soft matching where the treated entity's outcomes diverge from those of the control group, the fully efficient synthetic control method resulted in biased treatment impact estimates, and the traditional efficient synthetic control method led to highly variable results. To address these biases and instabilities, we developed a modified version of the efficient synthetic control method that involves a version of the filtered least absolute deviations pointwise optimal matching (FLELAD-POM) algorithm which combines the capabilities of the fully efficient and missing match methods for estimating the treatment impact using synthetic control. The results from simulated data sets show that the filtered method can effectively reduce the bias and variability associated with the treatment impact estimates obtained by the fully efficient synthetic control method. The method also handles the challenge of the treated entity's post-treatment dynamics when used in conjunction with multiple bases including counterfactual data for GDP per capita in Germany following the treatment of secession. Recent investigations have highlighted deep neural networks' susceptibility to adversarial inputs. However, existing countermeasures are largely insufficient. In this paper, we establish that a particular architecture of neural networks, utilizing identity mappings, has a theoretical limit to contain errors stemming from malicious interference. However, in practical applications, this network's ability to contain adversarial threats is largely ineffective. These findings imply that a neural network's capacity to contain adversarial threats is not solely determined by its architecture, but also factors such as the dataset, data distribution, input preprocessing, and the domain expert's intended specifications. Moreover, we demonstrate how the natural resilience of a neural network can be attributed to its solution of an optimal transport problem between the predicted output and the label, current state, and domain knowledge. In this context, domain knowledge is viewed as continuous and bounded. These observations prompt us to explore how the inherent resilience of a neural network can be enhanced through domain-centric approaches that maximize a neural network's (natural) robustness to malicious interference. A particular technique known as domain refinement proves effective in reducing adversarial threats by incorporating an optimized version of domain knowledge that is differentiated from original domain knowledge and is continuous, bounded, and more robust. This is achieved through either selecting an optimal version of domain knowledge that minimizes threats or through refining original domain knowledge to enhance the network's natural resilience. Experimental findings indicate that incorporating refined domain knowledge in Neural ODEs significantly minimizes adversarial threats with only marginal losses in accuracy on clean data, providing an efficient alternative to parameter-based approaches to robustness. The code for this paper can be found on the GitHub repository https://github.com/louismelou/DeepNeuralOptimalTransport. Additionally, we note that these findings provide an analytical understanding of why adversarial countermeasures in Deep Neural Networks have been largely ineffective. A neural network's solution of an optimal transport problem provides an insightful interpretation of its behavior, pinpoints the source of its fragility, and highlights the inherent impossibility of completely eliminating adversarial threats through a neural network's architecture design. Moreover, it emphasizes the importance of incorporating domain-centric approaches to robustness that prioritize understanding and incorporating domain knowledge to mitigate threats. Finally, these findings suggest the possibility that fragility may be a necessary price to pay for achieving a necessary level of accuracy on specific tasks, underscoring potential trade-offs between accuracy and robustness, and highlighting the limitations of current DNN-based systems. These additional contributions and findings can be found in an accompanying technical report Melou et al. 202

Therefore, we propose that total correlation can serve as a promising tool for developing accurate and data-driven models of functional connectivity in the brain. Historically, garbage collection has been used in functional languages, while imperative languages increasingly utilize type systems to safeguard memory usage. Our investigation applies existing methods for linear capabilities to ensure safe access to reference types that can be copied, with a particular emphasis on its novel extension to languages with tracing garbage collection, as well as data structures featuring explicit lifespan management. This work is related to hybrid programming that combines linear and non-linear elements, specifically in the context of the languages Rust and JavaScript. Our study is conducted through the modification of existing type systems, utilizing the $\pi$ type system for the description of linear resources. This involves defining a $\pi_{garbage\_col}$ extension that accommodates partial linear resources subject to garbage collection, with explicit deallocation ensuring memory safety. This extension is applied to the description of ciao, a multi-threaded functional language leveraging garbage collection, initially developed within the WAM framework, with initial results confirming its soundness. This extension is further validated in the description of C\#, a class-based, object-oriented language featuring safe deallocation, with the utilization of $\pi_{garbage\_col}$ confirming the adequacy of the proposed approach. This research contributes to the integration of programming languages with different memory management schemes by providing methods to translate and interpret various combinations of linear and non-linear references. While initially developed for languages incorporating explicit deallocation, this study also explores its application to languages featuring tracing garbage collection, with initial results confirming its soundness in both scenarios. This work is particularly relevant to hybrid programming that combines linear and non-linear elements, with initial evaluations indicating its increased expressiveness compared to the standard garbage collection approach. A technique combining K-means clustering with Voronoi tessellations in 3D produces the necessary input for SDF generation. By quantifying its performance using a multi-step cell tracking task, we found that models trained with our synthesis method outperformed baseline models in accurately localizing a moving cell's boundary from a partial view. The influence of stellar activity on exoplanet transit spectroscopy is a critical concern, and determining its impact will help determine if observed features are a result of the planet's composition or the star's characteristics. We used the ULTRACAM filterless imaging mode to observe 19 main-sequence stars with a range of activities levels, and analyzed their flux variations to determine how they change based on the star's rotational period and activity level. We then developed equations that relate the equivalent width of H2O bands and the level of stellar activity, and found that in order to accurately identify H2O in low-mass stars with varying activity levels, activity must be less than 10% of the stellar radius or less than 1000 ppm in flux. Finally, we proposed a technique using B-band data to assess the stellar activity and determine a signal-to-noise ratio needed to accurately identify H2O in low-mass stars. This study will aid in planning and interpreting future missions such as the James Webb Space telescope in preparing for exoplanet transit spectroscopy. The ULTRACAM data presented here provide a baseline for validating models that simulate stellar activity and predicting its influence on low-mass star spectra. It will also help develop analytical methods to remove the stellar signal in spectroscopy and determine accurate molecular abundances in exoplanet atmospheres. The data collected will aid in the selection of suitable planetary test objects for future missions. The fourth Industrial Revolution has significantly improved industrial productivity and competitiveness by incorporating data analytics and cyber-physical systems. Despite the benefits, both traditional and cyber-physical systems are plagued by uncertainties due to uncertain demand, availability of resources, and estimated production costs. resulting in delayed deliveries, inaccurate budget predictions, and reduced profitability. A novel approach to tackling uncertainty-driven problems in manufacturing is proposed, which integrates soft computing methods with a descriptionist framework. The proposed framework utilizes a generalized descriptionist approach as the core algorithm, combined with a trapezoidal membership function, and an ant colony optimization algorithm for knowledge acquisition and updating. The algorithm's key strengths are its ability to learn and adapt quickly, especially when dealing with dynamic problems in real-time. The effectiveness and reliability of the proposed framework were validated through comprehensive experimental simulations conducted using MATLAB software. The outcome demonstrates the framework's capability to tackle uncertainty-driven problems effectively and efficiently. The proposed framework's novel integration of a descriptionist algorithm with a trapezoidal membership function and ant colony optimization algorithm for learning and adaptation contributes significantly to the field. The utility and robustness of the proposed framework have also been established. The outcome provides valuable insights and suggestions for tackling uncertainty-driven problems in manufacturing contexts. Radio sources powered by an Active Galactic Nucleus have significant magnetic fields influencing their polarization properties, affecting observations of plasma and contaminating cosmic microwave background measurements. Understanding the polarization-statistics relationship with source characteristics is essential. By analyzing large radio source samples from 1.4 GHz surveys, this study calculates the median fractional polarization in relation to angular size. It finds a strong correlation between polarization and source size below ~5", with a weaker correlation above ~8". The results indicate depolarization due to the host galaxy and surrounding environment. Additionally, the curvature of low-frequency radio spectra shows an inverse correlation with polarization. The findings have significant implications for planned observations of the cosmic microwave background using the Large Synoptic Survey Telescope and the Deep Cosmic Microwave Background Survey. They suggest that sources smaller than ~5" need to be de-polarized by an energy spectrum cutoff at ~230 keV, while sources larger than ~8" require cutoffs above ~330 keV. For intermediate sources, the spectrum is ambiguous. To accurately assess polarization noise for CMB observations, the research suggests considering the distribution of polarization values rather than the median value. This leads to revised estimates of the angular scales necessary to achieve a specific level of polarization noise for the LSST-CMB project. We develop a class of stochastic advection problems to investigate turbulent transport properties, where the flow field statistics are represented as a continuous time Markov process. This representation accurately captures turbulence's essence, characterized by the shift from one coherent structure to another. Our analysis confirms the intermittency of the transport property, as validated by the increase in the scalar's variance in space, along with the scaling law of the transit-time distribution. Furthermore, we find that the exponential increase in the transit time is universal, across different flow regimes, despite the velocity field's intermittency varying across different classes. Additionally, we identify three distinct regimes in the transit-time distribution: classical Gaussian for small times, Whittle-Minimax for intermediate times, and a power-law for large times, which we associate with the coherent structures' sizes and lifetimes. Ultimately, we derive the Fickian transport coefficient from the stochastic model, as well as its corresponding diffusion time, striking an analogy between the eddy visit time and the time it takes for a molecule to leave the advection domain. Theoretical estimates for the diffusion coefficient and coefficient of variation have been performed for three flows: linear shear layer, the localist ABC flow, and Holmboe's unstable layer, demonstrating explicit comparisons with direct numerical simulations. The proposed model bears potential for application to a broad range of problems in geophysical and astrophysical flows by accounting for the transport properties of scalar fields. The model, along with its code, can be accessed at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.51095. The potential for applying the proposed model to solve complex flow problems in geophysical and astrophysical contexts is significant, especially in scenarios where the coherent structures play a prominent role. This paper presents a comprehensive study on the electromagnetic radiation behavior in a thin conductor plate separated by two large parallel walls at a temperature $T$, where the plate's area is $A$ and the distance between the walls is $d$. We utilize $T$, $A$, and $d$ as primary parameters to calculate the free energy of the system by integrating over the plate the stress-energy-momentum tensor derived by Brown and Maclay. Both thermodynamic regimes, $kTd/\hbar c \gg 1$ and $kTd/\hbar c \ll 1$, are explored in depth, and the influence of the slab walls' boundary conditions on various thermodynamic quantities, previously considered ill-defined or trivial in ordinary blackbody thermodynamics, is demonstrated to produce well-defined or nontrivial values, referred to as "Casimir's effect". By thoroughly investigating these relationships, it's hypothesized that they may be verified experimentally. Furthermore, the stability of electromagnetic radiation in the slab is assessed, with results suggesting unusual thermodynamic stability compared to expected gas behavior. Specifically, the system displays "Casimir's stability", characterized by two distinct types: "Casimir's radiation stability" and "Casimir's radiation-forest stability". "Casimir's radiation stability" occurs when $kTd/\hbar c \gg 1$ and the system remains stable over a broad temperature range. "Casimir's radiation-forest stability" occurs when $kTd/\hbar c \ll 1$ and the system remains stable, with its free energy decreasing as $T$ increases, contrasting typical gas behavior where the free energy increases as $T$ increases. Additionally, the thermodynamic phase diagrams of the system are calculated and analyzed, where phases found to exist are the Casimir phase, the de Sitter phase, and two radiation phases, namely, the radiation-forest phase and the radiation-lattice phase. Nonetheless, unlike ordinary blackbody thermodynamics, the system does not exhibit the Casimir phase's counterpart, a phase previously identified as the Casimir gas. By thoroughly investigating these relationships, it's hypothesized that they may be verified experimentally. Finally, the electromagnetic radiation behavior in the slab is found to produce an unusual relationship between entropy and information, where the system does not adhere to the typical gas behavior or Maxwell's famous maxim. Specifically, the system displays the following unusual relationship: $S(q)=S(0)+\beta\sum_{i\in q}p_i\ln p_i-$

A highly sought-after component in autonomous driving, 3D point cloud-based place recognition excels in areas lacking GPS functionality and serves a pivotal role in lidar-based SLAM systems through the identification of recurring loops. The presented research introduces the NDT-Transformer approach, enabling real-time, large-scale place recognition using 3D point clouds. The methodology utilizes the 3D Normal Distribution Transform (NDT) representation to summarize dense point clouds into geometrical shape descriptions via probabilistic distributions. Subsequently, the novel NDT-Transformer network processes a set of 3D NDT cell representations to learn global descriptors enriched with both geometrical and contextual data. The final step entails descriptor matching via a query-database for the purpose of place recognition. The proposed method demonstrates an enhancement of 7.52% and 7.11% in top 1 and top 1% recall respectively over state-of-the-art methods, as validated on the Oxford Robotcar benchmark. Furthermore, the NDT-Transformer approach exhibits a notable advantage in scalability, robustness, and adaptability characteristics. Notably, it successfully handles the challenging task of learning from sparse and noisy child nodes, and its applicability extends beyond the realm of place recognition, encompassing tasks such as 3D object reconstruction. The code for this research has been made available on GitHub: https://github.com/geoyd/NDT-Transformer. Moreover, the NDT-Transformer approach has been successfully evaluated on the recently introduced NuT-TS dataset, catering to the demands of large-scale place recognition from sparse lidar point clouds. The results demonstrate the model's capacity to endure an increase in both ground point count (approx. 10.3 times) and rotation degrees (approx. 2.4 times) and show a notable advantage over the baseline method. The findings of this research suggest that the final NDT cell-based representation holds the ability to effectively learn from the geometrical structure of 3D objects, and the incorporation of a self-supervised transformer network leads to a realization of a robust and efficient single description learning strategy. The self-supervised aspect of the model has been validated by training the model on the Oxford Robotcar dataset alone, and the results of this experiment indicate that the model achieves a top 1% recall of 52.66% and 57.23% for the urban and campus scenes, respectively. In a single-hop beeping network, stations interact via one-bit messages to form a distributed communication system. We explore the distributed computing domain's two core challenges, naming and counting issues, and our objective is to refine existing algorithms to reduce their energy usage and processing speed. Our key contribution is the development of efficient, randomized algorithms that achieve optimal O(n log n) processing efficiency and O(log n) energy usage for n-station beeping networks, addressing both the naming and counting problems. These algorithms improve previous outcomes by reducing energy usage and processing speed. We establish a connection between energy usage, naming, and counting problems, revealing that determining the minimum energy required to solve these problems in a n-station beeping network is equivalent to solving the well-known Boolean Pythagorean triple problem. Furthermore, our naming algorithm demonstrates that solving this energy minimization problem in a distributed setting is at least as challenging as in the classical world, as it generalizes the Boolean Pythagorean triple problem. The foundation of our work lies in a novel, efficient algorithm that addresses the classic k-coloring problem with optimal O(n log n) processing efficiency in a single-hop beeping network. This insight enables the development of a second k-coloring algorithm, also with optimal O(n log n) processing efficiency, but using only O(log n) energy usage. We then leverage these k-coloring algorithms to address the naming and counting problems efficiently. Interestingly, while the k-coloring problem's energy usage doesn't diminish with n for the classic version, its distributed counterpart yields significant energy savings for n-station beeping networks. We also show that naming and counting problems can be solved within the given energy bounds while reducing processing speed to near-optimal, a significant improvement over previous outcomes. The cornerstone of our work is a new, efficient algorithm for the k-coloring problem, its connections, and properties for the naming and counting problems in a single-hop beeping network. The algorithms and their proof sketches are provided in an extended version of this paper, available at arXiv.oxid. archives/2103.12860. Using a combination of density functional calculations and the linearized Migdal-Eliashberg equations with the functional derivative approach, we analyzed how the density of states affects the behavior of H3S as a function of pressure between 162 and 250 GPa. Our results show that accounting for variable density of states accurately reproduces the experimental critical temperature, whereas the simple single-band Migdal-Eliashberg equations yield a predicted $T_{c}$ that is about 10% higher than the actual value. Additionally, we found that considering a temperature-independent density of states leads to an overestimation of $T_{c}$ similar to the simple model, indicating that temperature-induced changes in band structure do not substantially impact the material's behavior in this pressure range. Nevertheless, we suggest that at higher pressures, $T_{c}$ may begin to decline due to a phenomenon called band narrowing. Finally, we conducted a thorough examination of the assumptions underlying our model to verify that its predictions correspond to those of the full anisotropic Eliashberg equations. Our outcomes indicate that the simple single-band model provides a reasonably accurate representation of the behavior of H3S, probably due to the fact that the material's phonon spectrum consists mainly of a single prominent branch whose behavior does not require a more complex model to describe properly. This paper presents an innovative technique to create spatial boundaries for navigation in dynamic environments. In the field of autonomous driving and robotics, motion planning often relies on global plans created using metric maps. However, the transient nature of dynamic environments necessitates continuous re-mapping and the challenge of identifying and avoiding temporary obstacles. Inspired by human navigation, the proposed method utilizes scene understanding to derive environmental boundaries for navigation. A novel beam collision detector is developed to track vehicle motion and identify obstacles, which are then utilized to generate spatial boundaries for navigation. A sampling-based path planner is presented that incorporates these boundaries, demonstrated through case studies and a comparative evaluation with existing methods. Results show that the proposed technique outperforms state-of-the-art methods, while highlighting the need for further research on navigating dynamic environments without metric maps. In the context of multiuser MIMO, the task of jointly selecting users and precoding can be reformulated as recovering a signal with multiple degrees of sparsity from underdetermined systems of equations. By assuming that the different sparsity patterns exhibit a probabilistic relationship, the task becomes identifying a signal's group-wise sparse structure to achieve minimum norm reconstruction. A novel algorithm, the iterative shrinkage algorithm for group sparsity (ISAGS), has been proposed for identifying group sparsity in noisy settings. In the process, the sum of absolute values of grouped coefficients is used as a regularization term and the task becomes solving a regularized least squares problem. By analyzing the recovery guarantees, the proposed algorithm's ability to achieve perfect reconstruction in both noise-free and noisy cases has been demonstrated. Furthermore, the practical effectiveness of ISAGS has been evaluated through simulations, which also reveal its robustness to varying probabilities of group sparsity and correlations between the groups. Notably, the proposed algorithm has been shown to jointly select users and precoding at a lower computational cost than existing methods. A possible extension of the algorithm to address the joint user selection and precoding problem in cognitive radio networks is also discussed. This network communication example complements the existing electrical engineering application of group sparsity, which involves compressive sampling at the Lee Laboratory. The connection between unconventional superconductivity, antiferromagnetism and nematic order in iron-based superconductors is still the subject of controversy. While in most FeSCs superconductivity arises close to a nematic and magnetic state, the iron-based compound LiFeAs exhibits unique characteristics, becoming superconducting below 18 K without undergoing a nematic and antiferromagnetic phase transition. Notably, recent studies using resonant inelastic x-ray scattering on single crystals of this material have yielded results contradicting previously reported findings, with single crystal data showing a strong and geometrically consistent continuum at around 130 meV and 160 meV, and contradicting the proposed superconducting pair formation and relaxation rates. These findings are discussed in relation to time-dependent spin-fluctuations and consider the impact of crystal field splitting on these properties. Further analysis using single particle spectroscopy from scanning tunneling microscopy has not provided direct evidence for magnon scattering affecting superconductivity, with the observed single particle density of states showing a weak increase at around 0.130 eV, and further discussion on possible origins of this phenomenon in line width has been provided. Ultimately, these findings highlight the need for continued research into the roots of superconductivity in LiFeAs, with the data presented potentially serving as a benchmark for comparing different simulation methods in studies of this material. One of the widely applied optimization methods in machine learning is Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD), which tackles optimization problems by iteratively selecting and computing gradients of small data subsets before updating the solution. When executed in parallel, SGD demands communication among involved processes at each iteration. Our innovation is a communication-optimizing approach for utilizing SGD to solve logistic regression. This strategy organizes computations into a pattern where communication is required only every $s$ iterations, as determined by the $s$ tuning parameter. By deriving theoretical bounds on operations count, data transfer rates, and latency, and accompanied by experimental findings, we demonstrate that the optimal SGD pattern depends on specific problem settings and cluster configurations that vary greatly in real-world scenarios. Consequently, our results validate the efficacy and efficiency of our Communication-Avoiding SGD (CA-SGD) method, which achieves significant speedups for certain use cases, with speedup bounds theoretically predicted to reach up to $\min(i, p)s$. This suggests that, under specific cluster setups, speedups larger than the number of processes involved are possible. Moreover, we have observed in our tests that, when the parameter $s$ is constant, the acceleration factor grows with the increasing size of datasets and parallelism degree. This confirms our theoretical speedup bounds. Finally, our method, implemented in PetIT, is a scalable framework that achieves substantial time savings even when minimal communication is involved, and we present quantitative speedup and efficiency metrics. This new approach, designed to optimize communication, yields impressive results, and we anticipate it to substantially accelerate SGD-based training in numerous use cases where data size and parallel processing capabilities allow for significant time savings. With our approach, the acceleration factor increases as the parameter $s$ (number of iterations between communications) and number of processes increase. For instance, at a parameter $s$ of 10, speedups of up to 32 were achieved on 32 processes, and speedups of up to 64 were achieved on 64 processes. In contrast, our method yielded minimal speedup when the parameter $s$ was 1 (one communication step per SGD iteration) as it should be. Future large-scale radio interferometers, aiming to detect 21\,cm signals across vast distances, may struggle with computational demands traditional correlators pose. Implementing the Fourier Transform as part of correlator design could mitigate this problem by its efficient algorithm (the FFT) and significant reduction in hardware requirements. Despite FFT-based architectures being explored for real-time applications, there is currently a lack of clear guidance on implementing the FFT as part of interferometric correlators. This study assesses different FFT-nail technologies and their suitability for this application, taking into account traditional correlator data consumption as an optimization factor. The evaluation of 11 different FFT-based architectures reveals that, on average, they require approximately 61 percent fewer hardware resources than classical correlators, albeit with unique strengths (high data rates achievable with analog technologies versus high bandwidths with digital technologies). All the explored architectures were found to significantly reduce hardware resources compared to traditional Stage-1, Stage-2 and Standalone correlators. The investigation does, however, highlight that no single FFT-based architecture is clearly superior to classical designs. In practice, specific hardware resources requirements depend heavily on the specific radio interferometer in question. With the variability in distances between antennas ranging from a few metres to thousands of kilometres, it becomes apparent that there is currently no single optimal solution. All investigated FFT-based architectures were found to have considerable drawbacks as well (e.g. significant dispreading noise, loss of coherence, hardware complexity, loss of data folding efficiency, among others). In terms of the spread spectrum modulation techniques used, there is currently no FFT-based architecture assessed that can clearly outperform classical designs. In light of these findings, the question of whether and how FFT-based architectures can be utilized effectively to reduce resources requirements is posed as an area of further study and research. Moreover, potential ways to leverage advancements in FFT-based technologies and combine them with novel ideas in areas like folding techniques, channelization design, modulation techniques and post-processing methods to finally yield efficient and coherent observables. In other words, can the FFT-based architecture evolution be kick-started to finally yield classical designs' performance in interferometric observations. In summary, this study aims to provide a clear direction for researchers working on providing efficient and coherent interferometric observations with reduced resources. In practice, this research identified and assessed various FFT-based architectures and explored novel ideas to finally yield efficient and coherent observables with reduced resources. On the other hand, portfolio optimization techniques like the Black-Litterman method enable portfolio managers to benefit from their expertise and market insights, combining this with generative models like the Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) offers the potential for generative scenarios. Historically, GANs have been limited in their ability to capture complex patterns, but recent advancements in generative models such as the Generative Adversarial Transformer (GAT) have addressed this limitation and demonstrated better results. Action-CSA can be combined with techniques such as temperature schedules and path averaging to increase efficiency and accuracy. Following the success of pretraining techniques in learning representations, various methods utilizing pre-trained models in continual learning have been developed. Some of these methods build upon the pre-trained representations by implementing mechanisms for continual learning with minimal or no updates to the backbone models. In this study, we challenge the necessity of complex mechanisms for continuing to learn with pre-trained models, particularly those that receive minimal updates. We also demonstrate that a basic, pre-trained model can achieve state-of-the-art results in continual learning tasks involving image classification. We compare the existing, elaborate continue-to-learn methods (including Loso, BIM, BIL, and FCM) with a simple approach involving pre-trained features frozen in place. We perform this analysis on three image classification tasks that vary in complexity, including CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet-1K. Notably, a simplified, pre-trained model resulted in comparable or higher baseline accuracy compared to more complex methods in two out of three evaluation scenarios. We also investigated the properties of the pre-trained features, including their calibrability and similarity to human confidence ratings. Notably, a calibration-based metric indicated a pre-trained DNN's responses were no longer well-calibrated after transfer, suggesting that well-trained models do not necessarily remain well-calibrated when exposed to new data. Furthermore, the pre-trained features' distribution of human-like confidence ratings ( Chernoff Goodness) was used to assess their human-like quality in two scenarios, and it was found that the feature assessments that deviated from human-like confidence, such as those obtained through Kalman Filter implementations, did not impede the pre-trained model's performance in classification tasks. We also found that the feature assessments that deviated from human-like confidence significantly increased the model entropy, as measured by the pre-trained feature distribution's cross-entropy. In summary, a basic, pre-trained model can achieve state-of-the-art results in continual learning tasks, highlighting the need for further research to understand why elaborate continue-to-learn methods, particularly those that implement memory and other mechanisms, do not necessarily outperform a simple approach involving pre-trained features frozen in place. Future work could explore the feature assessments that do not mimic human-like confidence but still result in well-calibrated responses and good performance in continual learning tasks. As social media increasingly influences public perceptions globally, researchers have focused on tackling the pervasive issue of hate speech online. This pernicious problem gives rise to real-world consequences, such as heightened social divisions and violent crimes. Previous studies on hate speech detection within social media texts have been conducted, yet they often relied on existing datasets which were either limited in scope or inadequate for quality. Moreover, existing research often solely employed description-based training data, neglecting the value of annotations that also considered the post's context. The goal of this paper is to address these gaps by introducing a novel dataset dubbed HateSpeechMobil, which is designed for task-oriented machine learning and incorporates a comprehensive dataset comprising 15,999 annotated English tweets rated by native speakers. Additionally, we examine various text-only features, including linguistic and linguistic-cognitive characteristics, for predicting hate speech. Our experiments show that simply leveraging these local text features enables us to achieve an accuracy of 90.95% using a binary classification approach. Moreover, our results suggest that incorporating transfer learning-based word embeddings improves performance while also validating their cross-lingual applicability. Finally, our findings indicate that MobiliNet, which is a neural network model for classifying in-line hate speech, is both efficient and effective. Our dataset, which can be accessed via https://github.com/alejo Penalto/HateSpeechMobil, is meant to support researchers in advancing hate speech detection within social media domains. Our goal is that these results will help bridge the gap between machine learning and natural language processing communities and promote more robust hate speech recognition systems in real-world applications. Ultimately, our ultimate goal is to contribute to reducing social divisions and violent crimes worldwide. We explore the behavior of large networks of theta neurons, deriving degree-based mean field equations that capture the overall dynamics of these networks. By assuming random connections, we analyze the effects of varying in- and out-degree distribution widths on synaptically and gap junction coupled networks. Our findings reveal that the out-degree distribution has no impact on synaptically coupled network dynamics. Broadening the in-degree distribution of inhibitory networks eliminates oscillations and narrows the bistability range in excitatory networks. Conversely, in gap junction coupled networks, in-degree distribution variations shift the onset points for collective oscillations. Many of these results persist in networks of more biologically accurate neurons. Additionally, we observe reduced width and shifted onset points of collective oscillations in bi-stable networks with increasing out-degree distribution width. These findings offer valuable insights for designing spiking neural networks that can mimic synchronized neural oscillations. Moreover, they may guide researchers in selecting suitable neuron models and degree distribution profiles for networks involving real neurons. Finally, our work identifies possibilities and limitations of mean field analysis in networks of neurons. Although generally applicable, this approach fails in networks of a specific class of biologically realistic neuron, requiring further modification. Our code is available online for replication purposes.

The timely detection of COVID-19 remains a significant research priority, offering potential advantages in the initial stages of an outbreak. Advanced methods to screen for infections have been well-integrated into pandemic response strategies, also helping to reduce hospital workloads. In contrast, post-infection replication detection methods that identify carriers just entering their infectious periods remains a relatively under-explored area. This study focuses on developing a system to detect COVID-19 patients in late infection stages, employing a combination of real-time PCR capabilities and asymptotic statistical detection techniques. We propose a 'test-on-suspect' approach, involving repeated testing of probable infectants until a positive result is obtained. This leads to a bivariate Ber-nolli success model and a comparative analysis of different infection period distributions. Furthermore, this detection system is assessed under uncertain epidemiological conditions and multiple testing scenarios. We conclude that while this detection method cannot completely eliminate infection risks, it can significantly reduce the odds of transmission and slow the spread of the epidemic if implemented early in an outbreak. In contrast, late implementation of this detection method after the epidemic peaks has a limited impact on transmission dynamics. Nonetheless, late implementation can still alleviate the pressure on healthcare systems if mortality rates are considered. This detection method also cannot completely eliminate 'deadly zoom-in' effects of high transmission rates on hospitalizations, infections, hospitalizations, and mortality rates. Nevertheless, a systematic 'test-on-suspect' detection approach can help mitigate this phenomenon to some extent. This detection method has the potential to reduce the value of the transmission risk parameter by as much as 64.8% in the event of an outbreak and up to 43.1% when the epidemic has peaked. In general, this detection method is effective in reducing the peak transmission rates of the disease. In countries lacking a functional public health system, replication detection may not effectively reduce transmission rates, resulting in limited delays to inevitable hospitalizations, infections, and mortality rates, and an increased pressure on healthcare systems. In contrast, replication detection may not effectively reduce transmission rates in countries with a well-established public health system, resulting in limited delays to inevitable hospitalizations, infections, and mortality rates, and an increased pressure on healthcare systems. This detection method is generally more effective when implemented early in an outbreak and has the potential to significantly reduce the pressure on healthcare systems if implemented late in an epidemic. In countries with existing public health systems, replication detection may not effectively reduce transmission rates, however, it can help alleviate the pressure on healthcare systems if implemented late in an epidemic.

A Graph Neural Network (GNN) is an effective neural network architecture that processes graph data, extensively applied across multiple domains. Unlike traditional neural network models, GNN can operate in a decentralized manner, facilitating communication among neighboring nodes and potentially leading to more efficient control mechanisms in wireless communication systems. However, wireless channel disruptions significantly reduce the robustness of GNN predictions. To overcome this limitation, we develop methods to assess the robustness of decentralized GNN predictions in various wireless communication systems, focusing on a binary classification model. We evaluate GNN performance in both unencoded and encoded systems, then propose innovative retransmission techniques to address data transmission errors and improve GNN robustness. Our research involves simulation-based validation on synthetic graph data, demonstrating the effectiveness of our retransmission mechanisms and providing valuable insights for practical applications. The results show that using our retransmission techniques can achieve up to 100% recovery of GNN predictions in the presence of errors. Moreover, we observe that decoding success rate reaches above 95% when using retransmission is prioritized over GNN robustness in the unencoded system, and this rate reaches above 93% in the encoded system. The proposed retransmission techniques outperform traditional retransmission methods, such as those employed in IEEE 802.16 and IEEE 802.11 protocols. To showcase the practical relevance of our research, we demonstrate how our retransmission techniques can improve GNN robustness in real-world applications, including edge computing-based traffic management and covert communication systems. The presented findings and algorithms provide valuable insights for effectively utilizing GNN in communication systems and may be adapted to other applications. The accompanying source code, available at https://github.com/ WirelessRobustnessGNN, facilitates reproducible research. The code supports multiple frameworks, including PyTorch, PyGNN, and FMBP, and includes benchmarks for synthetic graph data, including Correlation-based Graphs, Erdos-Renyi Graphs, and Barabasi-Albert Graphs. The repository includes the decentralized training code for the GNN model using PyGNN, as well as the implementation of the retransmission techniques using SimPy, a Python engineering simulation framework. The research data, including graph samples, is stored in a separate repository https://github.com/Multigrid-Based-PyGNNGraphSamples. The findings from this research may be extended to improve the robustness of other neural network models, such as transformer-based architectures, in the future. In the broader South American context, Brazil ranks third for its homicide death toll behind only Venezuela and Colombia.  In assessing the consequences of violent acts, an analysis of both public health systems and the country's justice systems is required in addition to other essential components.  Focusing specifically on the Goias region in the country's Central-West, a concerning increase from 24.5 per 100,000 people to 42.6 per 100,000 people in the span from 2002 to 2014 has led researchers to analyze this phenomenon using available socio-demographic information for the state and applying correlation analysis, as well as employing three clustering algorithms: Hierarchical, K-means, and Density-based methods. The study reveals that high homicide rates have become a feature of cities located close to larger metropolitan areas despite those cities boasting superior socio-economic indicators. Furthermore, an evaluation of annual homicide trends reveals that cities may be classified into three distinct clusters based on their homicide rates. The research offers insights for the goias regional administration to reevaluate its security and public health strategies and address the complex challenges presented by urban violence. Interestingly, a comparison with other Brazilian states reveals that Goias exhibits distinct patterns of homicide trends and levels across the entire Brazilian context. The research code and analysis results have been released through open-source platforms, an open-data strategy also supported by the Brazilian Government. The study's findings and methodology have been made available to inform-related research through the activation of a data-sharing agreement. Axions emerge as a logical outcome of the Peccei-Quinn mechanism, the leading explanation for the strong-CP issue.  Variants of axions known as axion-like particles (ALPs) also arise in various modifications of the Standard Model, particularly in string theories.  Both axions and ALPs have compelling justifications as potential components of Dark Matter (DM), and substantial quantities would be generated at the Sun's core.  For nearly two decades, the CAST experiment at CERN has been one of the primary efforts to detect axions.  The International Axion Observatory (IAXO) is an enhanced, large-scale version of axion-hunting technology, aimed at further refining searches for solar axions or ALPs, achieving an elevated signal-to-background ratio of roughly 5 orders of magnitude.  

We now provide an overview of astrophysical signs and theoretical models within the context of axions and ALPs, as well as the primary focuses and tools for data analysis in searching for these particles. 

Recent, more detailed studies based on years worth of data collected by IAXO are then presented: these focus on different aspects such as sensitivity, precision and completeness, as well as initial search results from practice runs in 2019 and 2020. 

Lastly, we examine the broader range of astroparticle research involving axions/ALPs in relation to astroparticle physics and future prospects for IAXO-related studies and third-generation axion/ALP experiments. 

Note: This article is based on a talk given at FEYCAN 2020 and includes an introduction to IAXO's primary objective, followed by a summary of its scientific findings, as well as a look at the broader range of astroparticle research focusing on axions/ALPs, and the third-generation experiments.  The closing section contains additional information, including a summary of IAXO's scientific findings and astroparticle research, as well as potential future challenges and opportunities, given the COVID-19 pandemic context.  We wish to express our gratitude towards the organizers for this opportunity and the participants for their engagement, and hope this summary might foster increased awareness among the FEYCAN community about the IAXO project and its accomplishments.

Our research examined the connection between initial anisotropic geometry and anisotropic flow within a multiphase transport model, specifically for 200 GeV Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. Contrary to elliptical flow's dependence on centrality, we discovered minimal variation in triangular flow centrality. However, once the influence of initial geometry was removed, we observed an increase in $v_3/\epsilon_3$ in proportion to transverse particle density, mirroring $v_2/\epsilon_2$'s behavior. Additionally, we found triangular and elliptical flow to exhibit analogous transverse momentum dependencies for identified particles. These outcomes are in line with expectations based on the initial anisotropic geometry's characteristics. In an effort to simplify the underlying flow dynamics, we developed a model incorporating both initial anisotropic geometry and parton-phase description, successfully reproducing measured $v_2$ and $v_3$ in Au+Au collisions. The model's framework allows for the determination of the parton-phase description's initial anisotropic geometry via input parameters such as the initial radial flow velocity and elliptical flow magnitude. Ultimately, our analysis provides evidence that the initial anisotropic geometry plays a crucial role in anisotropic flow formation. It also lays a foundation for using anisotropic flow to probe the initial geometry of the initial media and the parton-phase description of high-energy heavy ion collisions. Further research may leverage $v_3$'s sensitivity to initial anisotropic geometry to probe the initial media of 200 GeV Ru+Ru collisions, a phenomenon currently unexplored in the scientific community. The observed enhancement of $v_3/\epsilon_3$ in 120 GeV Cu+Cu collisions may also warrant further exploration. The present analysis represents a crucial step towards understanding anisotropic flow through the lens of initial geometry and parton-phase description. Our proposed testbed, SyROF, is designed to facilitate the development of
cooperative robot systems, making it easily accessible for both undergraduate
and graduate students to implement robotic swarms in a timely manner. To achieve
this goal, we developed SyROF, an innovative testbed that features a user-friendly,
high-level programming environment supporting the Timed Input/Output Automata
(TIOA) paradigm. This versatile tool boasts the following distinctive features: 
1) An efficient synchronization mechanism to coordinate robotic actions, 
2) A membership verification system with built-in failure detection, and 
3) A transparent, common knowledge sharing platform. These key attributes
streamline the development of robotic swarms by addressing crucial implementation
challenges. Our testbed consists of a modular structure comprising five interdependent
layers: A lower layer utilizes a real-time communication system, followed by a Kalman filter
to accurately track the robot's location, orientation, and speed, and the upper layer,
incorporating a synchronizer to execute actions, disseminate common knowledge, and manage
failure occurrences, finally topped off by the programming environment itself. We
validate the SyROF testbed by demonstrating its capabilities by implementing a global
aggregation algorithm, showcasing its benefits and limitations. Moreover, SyROF is
accompanied by comprehensive didactic materials such as testbed activation tutorials,
sample codes, and instructional guides, which are readily available online. With SyROF, we
aim to inspire undergraduate and graduate students to explore the exciting field of
robotic swarms, promoting hands-on research into the design of efficient, cooperative
robot systems. Our ultimate goal is to expand SyROF's scope by integrating it with various
third-party software platforms and integrating it with wearable technology devices like smartwatches. In addition, we will develop a core educational program centered on the testbed, accompanied by didactic materials such as university course templates, research papers, and research videos.
