This study builds upon three significant lines of research related to dissimilarity-based clustering and integrates them into a unified framework that provides a principle-driven approach to clustering. Specifically, it draws from Jardine and Sibson's concept of overlapping clusters, Carlsson and M\'{e}moli's functorial approach to partition-based clustering, and the injective envelope theory of Isbell and Dress. Carlsson and M\'{e}moli's idea of treating clustering methods as functors that map metric spaces to clusters, subject to functoriality, has gained considerable influence in the field. However, a comprehensive theoretical framework incorporating overlapping clusters had yet to be developed, which this study seeks to address. A natural question arises regarding the criteria for convergence towards stable clusters when given a sequence of updates to the metric space, or the underlying clustering algorithm. This study develops a theory that provides new insights into this inquiry. A metric on the space of all possible clusters is defined that measures the dissimilarity between different clusterings. This metric has the beneficial property of being bounded below by the dissimilarity between any pair of points in a cluster. A new type of fuzzy cluster is introduced that includes many crisp clusters, along with the minimum fuzzy clusters that satisfy this criterion. It is demonstrated that the convergence towards stable clusters in various clustering algorithms, such as hierarchical and partition-based, can be achieved by applying the functorial clustering theory to metric spaces and sampling the metric space infinitely. A single theoretical framework is provided that unifies previously unrelated results from the field. Additionally, it is demonstrated that the consistency of clustering algorithms like single-linkage and the relaxed $k$-means is ensured when sampling infinitely from the metric space, or the sample size tends to infinity. A novel connection between the relaxed $k$-means and the injective cluster is developed, including the comprehensive study of the structure and properties of the injective cluster. A new type of diagram also is introduced that represents the mapping of metric spaces to clusters, subject to functoriality, along with the diagram's properties and relationships to the relaxed $k$-means clustering. A theoretical study of the relaxed $k$-means for samples of infinite size, or the sample's order tends to infinity, is developed using the diagram's congruent morphisms. Tensor completion techniques seek to recover incomplete data in observed tensors by leveraging their low-rank properties, particularly useful in visual data recovery applications. However, when dealing with sequential data such as streaming video, missing tensor entries need to be recovered in real-time without compromising performance. Existing streaming algorithms may not be effective when the data structure significantly changes over time, as seen in videos with rapid scene shifts or intense motion. This paper presents a groundbreaking, patch-based framework for completing tensors from streaming video. For each incoming frame, small image segments are identified by tracking them from the previous frame, and a unique tensor is created by combining similar segments from the new frame. This tensor is then restored using a real-time tensor completion algorithm. Our novel approach also introduces an enhanced patch tracking method for more efficient and accurate data recovery and a revised optimization algorithm to guarantee the new method's convergence. Comprehensive experiments on diverse video datasets reveal that this framework significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art tensor completion methods for both visual and near-infrared data restoration. Notably, it excels at processing multiple moving objects, significant scene changes, and fast motion while ensuring real-time performance. This research aims to inspire the development of more advanced online tensor completion algorithms for a wide range of applications. The proposed framework and source code are freely available for use in future research. This research has a new repository at: https://github.com/CFST-UF-vision/StreamingTensorCompletionCode.git. By combining traditional rendering techniques with neural networks, Deferred Neural
Rendering achieves a balance between computational simplicity and visually realistic
images. Extending DNR to use skinned meshes for rendering dynamic objects would
significantly enhance its applications. However, doing so requires accounting for
articulations, which would substantially increase the potential number of neural
models needed, making it impractical. In contrast, we propose Articulated Neural
Rendering (ANR), a new approach that uses a single universal model to handle
complex meshes with many articulations. ANR uses mesh-specific rendering
operations to ensure efficient and coherent rendering of highly articulated
meshes. Our method demonstrates a significant improvement for challenging
articularations not well-represented by standard neural networks, such as walking
and talking humans. An embedded version of ANR is also proposed, which can be
embedded into standard mesh-based animation systems, enabling real-time rendering
on resource-constrained devices. Our research presents a new direction for
applying neural networks to handle intricate mesh dynamics, allowing for a more
seamless integration of realistic rendering and traditional animation techniques.

Certain tangle diagrams associated with three strands that include AW generators reveal links through evaluation that match a predicted fusion table. This expected table is derived from the Askey-Wilson algebra's characteristics, specifically its fusion table. This evidence supports the hypothesis that the Askey-Wilson algebra is linked with SU(2) Chern-Simons theory at its Euler characteristic. It is also proposed that the Askey-Wilson algebra's characteristics could be used to calculate three-strand link invariants that match the predicted fusion table. Additionally, links that contain two strands with two holes are identified and their invariants derived; these matches exactly what would be predicted based on local diagram technology. Finally, analogs involving three strands with three holes are proposed and outlined. The study presented in this exploration offers new insight into the relationship between the local diagram technology and the Askey-Wilson algebra. One scenario considers the SIS model, which assumes susceptible individuals only revert to infected individuals who visit hospitals. When models are locked down, no pandemic occurs. However, removing lockdown measures in this case significantly increases the outbreak's size and severity. Conversely, a scenario based on the SIR model, which also takes into account recovered individuals, shows that the current pandemic does not align with this model. This discrepancy may be due to the underutilization of hospital capacities or a highly contagious virus, which could be a key factor in the current pandemic. We have also found that the time it takes for a population to recover, in the event of an outbreak, is much longer than one would expect based on the basic reproduction number. A study on stick-slip dynamics and the convergence of motion paths in systems governed by Coulomb friction is conducted. The existence of a universally accessible and attractive region, near an equilibrium state, is confirmed through analytical means. Theoretical findings reveal that the system can only converge asymptotically, involving multiple sequences of stick-slip cycles, regardless of the starting conditions. Numerical simulations, in various dimensions and scenarios with diverse coefficients of friction, along with disparate types of external forces (perfection, impulse, continuous), illustrate the theoretical concepts and multiple convergent trajectories. The attractive regions for convergence are mapped and described; specifically, evidence of multiple sequences of stick-slip cycles, even in 1D systems with persistent forces, is presented. Furthermore, the possibility of system re-attractivity after temporary stabilization is explored through analysis of the stick-slip transition process. Theoretical findings, along with the presented counterexamples, challenge the prevalent notion that Coulomb friction leads to the convergence of motion paths towards an ideal, frictionless trajectory. Theoretical means to predict the sequences of stick-slip cycles, potentially allowing for the assessment of frictional losses, are also discussed. The theoretical framework developed may be applied to more intricate frictional systems, involving multi-degree-of-freedom movements, to investigate the convergence of motion paths under varying external influences and frictional forces. The theoretical means to predict convergence for general multi-body movement systems, along with the associated frictial losses, are explored. The study suggests the existence of sequences featuring an increasing number of slip cycles, potentially lasting indefinitely, and calls for the careful re-evaluation of the notion that Coulomb friction necessarily leads to the convergence of motion paths towards an ideal, frictionless trajectory. The theoretical means to predict the sequences of stick-slip cycles, potentially allowing for the assessment of frictional losses, are discussed along with numerical simulations that confirm the theoretical findings and showcase the particular cases and scenarios in which the theoretical results are verified. The study may be extended to more intricate frictional systems, involving multi-degree-of-freedom movements, to investigate the convergence of motion paths under varying external influences and frictional forces. The theoretical framework developed may lead to novel methods for calculating frictional losses in complex multi-body movement systems. The proposed approach, based on the study of Coulomb friction, can be applied to general contact scenarios, involving frictional forces, to predict the convergence of motion paths and potential losses, potentially shedding light on the critical aspects of contact mechanics. A novel reinforcement learning method based on the actor-critic type has been developed to tackle portfolio hedging challenges for a variety of financial securities and derivatives using historical data only. Key aspects of this approach involve leveraging various derivative types such as forwards, futures, options, and taking into account factors such as trading costs, liquidity constraints and soft constraints. This technique effectively handles portfolio hedging for multiple objectives, considering trading costs and constraints, thereby resulting in optimal risk-neutral valuation with minimal costs. Furthermore, the approach can easily adapt to various financial environments and assets with no need for market observations, making it highly practical for use in real-world financial scenarios. Experimental results demonstrate that this method outperforms traditional derivative pricing methods such as the Black-Scholes and Binomial models. Additionally, the approach's ability to handle non-trivial settings even with a limited time horizon was verified, suggesting its potential to tackle more complex problems in the future. This research's findings showcase the effectiveness of using reinforcement learning to tackle portfolio hedging and risk-neutral valuation challenges. They also reveal the need for further investigation into how to utilize the actor-critic method effectively in order to tackle a variety of objectives and factors in more complex scenarios. Furthermore, the approach's potential to leverage multi-agent reinforcement learning and extend it to tackle portfolio management and hedging challenges in more complex environments is also discussed. Lastly, the research's findings may explain why current reinforcement learning models are not yet robust enough to tackle real-world financial challenges.

The reducible double confluent Heun equation stands out due to its unique unfolding into a Fuchsian equation through a general symmetric process. The Fuchsian equation resulting from the unfolding of this particular DCHE has five distinct singular points: three located near a vanishing parameter value, one corresponding to infinity, and another positioned at its reciprocal, as well as a fifth point at infinity. The monodromy matrix of the equation near a specific regular resonant singularity at the origin can be demonstrated to emerge as a limiting product of the monodromy matrices at singular points resulting from the unfolding of the equation's parameters. The monodromy matrix near another irregular singularity at the origin shows a specific limit behavior; importantly, this matrix remains non-singular under specific conditions related to the monodromy matrices at the other regular singular points. The results are further validated through specific examples involving Jacobi polynomials and Bessel functions. The findings provide a foundation for further research on the matrix equation in question, particularly regarding its solutions, which are expressed using integrals involving the hypergeometric function ${_0F_1}$ and its derivatives. The given solutions are consistent with those obtained using other approaches, such as the Fock-Fock Bethe lattice method. The equation stands out due to its unique representation among all DCHEs; interestingly, the given examples indicate that some general properties observed in the equation may not be broadly applicable to the larger class of DCHEs. Low-rank matrix recovery issues with complex high-dimensional data are ubiquitous in statistical and machine learning domains. This research investigates the theoretical recovery boundaries for a wide range of such problems. We specifically address the problem of estimating a matrix of rank one from observations with differing Gaussian noise levels across various matrix components. We derive exact formulas for the mean squared error in matrix and factor estimation in an infinite-dimensional setting where a fixed number of matrix components is examined. These findings are based on an innovative model transformation from the homogeneous to a heterogeneous low-rank matrix tensor product model. We demonstrate that some PCA-based methods are optimal in certain scenarios but suboptimal in others. Numerical experiments comparing these findings with PCA-based methods and other optimization techniques such as gradient descent and message passing are also provided. When the matrix rank increases, we extend these results for Gaussian noise levels to a finite sample case and use a combination of techniques from asymptotic analysis and interpolation. We derive interpolation-based recovery bounds similar to the infinite-dimensional setting. Moreover, we show that PCA-based methods perform optimally (or very close to optimal) in both the finite and infinite-dimensional settings. We compare these results with the recently introduced rank-one matrix recovery bounds using spectral truncation. Our findings indicate that PCA-based methods are optimal when the matrix rank increases, but they are suboptimal in scenarios with low noise levels and few observed matrix blocks. We use numerical experiments to demonstrate the superiority of the proposed recovery bounds over existing models. We apply these results to the context of multi-block sparse recovery, showing that the optimal recovery bounds can be achieved by cross-regularizing distinct block estimates. We provide supporting numerical evidence for this conclusion. The proposed recovery bounds are represented as preprint. A public code for the project is available at the provided link. We extend the heterogeneous low-rank matrix tensor product model to address the recovery of graph four-closures in network analysis. We utilize the derived recovery bounds to answer open questions about the optimal sample size required to achieve exact recovery of a graph four-closure under noise conditions. This research is an extension of previous CRIST studies that addressed the recovery of a single block of a low-rank matrix and the recovery of a graph two-closure. We provide the derived recovery bounds for the general tensor product model and offer numerical evidence to confirm our findings. Our results indicate that the optimal sample size four-fold increases as the density of the graph decreases. In this research, we examine the vibrational spectrum of a constrained ring, taking note of its distinct properties that defy symmetry expectations inherent to topological models. A unique characteristic arises due to 2nd-order exceptional points, where an otherwise trivial band structure becomes topologically complex at higher energy levels. Absence of traditional symmetry in the model allows the emergence of fractional boundary states in the system. Moreover, another key aspect of the bulk-boundary correspondence is uncovered, where an extra band in the bulk spacetime correlates with boundary states in the system. Besides the fundamental aspects of the fractional MPZ model, we also investigate more complex versions of the model, including those with different types of constraints and interactions with a bosonic bath. Ultimately, this research aims to connect the resulting topological model with experimentally feasible setups, such as optomechanical systems. Note that a related version of the model with exactly solvable dynamics, where the Hamiltonian commutes with the lattice's translation, has been reported in another study. In contrast, we focus here on the contrary scenario, where there is no such symmetry, and consequently, the dynamics can only be approximated. A notable aspect of the resulting model is that it supports anomalous slow dynamics, characterized by a time scale proportional to N^2, where N is the number of the mpz's sites. This research initially discovered and analyzed the dynamics of a single MPZ in the strong coupling regime with a single bosonic site. It was found there that a notable aspect of the resulting model is that it supports anomalous slow dynamics, where the time scale of the process is proportional to the 7th power of the ratio between the mpz's frequency and that of the bosonic site. For this reason, we believe that it is feasible to establish a connection between the resulting topological model and possible experimental setups, such as optomechanical systems. Note, as an alternative scenario, we also examined more complex versions of the MPZ model, including those with different types of constraints and interactions, where two notable aspects emerged: the dynamics can be approximated by considering the transfer of energy between the topological bulk and non-topological boundaries, where the rate of this process is proportional to the 2nd power of the ratio between the mpz's frequency and that of the bosonic site. We introduce the semi-inclusive Lepton Flavour Universality ratio, $R_s$, to verify electron-to-muon universality in the $b \to s \ell^+ \ell^-$ process at $e^+ e^-$ $B$-meson facilities. The $R_s$ quantity can be calculated using the hadronic final state invariant mass and the same energy lepton for any $b \to s \ell^+ \ell^-$ process, thereby allowing for detailed comparison with Standard Model predictions. We analyze $B \to X_s e^+ e^-$ data from KEKB in this context. According to our analysis, most $b \to s \ell^+ \ell^-$ processes exhibit agreement with Standard Model predictions within two standard deviations, but $R_s$ values for higher energy lepton moments show slight discrepancies. We predict that upcoming experiments at $e^+ e^-$ $B$-meson facilities, such as CEPC and FCC-ee, will be able to confirm or challenge the current Standard Model predictions with 95% confidence levels. Additionally, we propose that $R_s$ can identify new physics potentially present in $b \to s \ell^+ \ell^-$ processes at $b$-factory energy levels. Finally, we note that $R_s$ offers standardization for comparison across various $b \to s \ell^+ \ell^-$ processes, thereby allowing for fresh insights into these processes. Moreover, its calculation from $b \to s \ell^+ \ell^-$ data offers comparative advantages over contributions from $b \to s \gamma$ processes. We believe that these properties make $R_s$ a versatile and valuable tool for fresh analysis and investigation in the context of $b \to s \ell^+ \ell^-$ processes at $e^+ e^-$ $B$-meson facilities. In order to present these findings in a consolidated manner, we have prepared a public code for the $R_s$ ratio at $e^+ e^-$ $B$-meson facilities, thereby allowing for fresh, not fully-exploited data from standard universality processes at $e^+ e^-$ collider facilities to be analyzed and studied. This study presents a novel approach to designing distributed output-feedback controllers for interconnected systems with constrained agent interactions. Each agent's controller is autonomously configured based on its locally available data, leading to a decentralized design. Importantly, our approach can maintain stability even in the face of dynamic network reconfigurations, without requiring adjustments from other agents, thus ensuring seamless integration of new members and efficient controller upkeep. This robust design is enabled by leveraging Bass' algorithm to compute stabilizing controller gains through distributed solutions to Lyapunov equations. Our approach is demonstrated via a comprehensive example, specifically a 13-agent system. Furthermore, we propose a centralized method for assessing individual agent controller stability and provide corresponding conditions. Key advantages of our design include its flexibility to handle various agent sizes and network topologies, leading to a scalable solution. This design framework is versatile and applicable to a wide range of networked systems including smart grids, data centers, transportation systems, and cyberphysical systems. Moreover, it can accommodate diverse controller structures such as linear controllers or those with fuzzy and neural components. It is flexible enough to be applied to problems where output feedback is required but not feasible, replacing it with state feedback or input fuzzy feedback if necessary. Lastly, it is compatible with problems involving incomplete or sparse network connectivity. Online implementation of the design requires an estimated error-correction mechanism to account for plant-model mismatch and changing network conditions to ensure robust output tracking and robust tracking output feedback. The distributed design framework is shown to be effective in achieving robust output tracking and robust tracking output feedback for systems with arbitrary network topologies and flexible agent sizes. Online learning of the design based on an adaptation mechanism is possible and proposed, leading to a stable adaptive controller. We've developed a COVID-19 diagnosis framework that uses CT scan image analysis with a double feature extraction technique via BERT. The initial step utilizes a 3D-CNN to extract spatial information from the CT images and then employs BERT for temporal aggregation of these features. A classification model is trained on randomly sampled CT volumes, and subsequent steps utilize the network to extract embedding features from the original scan. Averaging the embedding features from random samples yields a representative feature for the entire CT scan, and both are used in combination for classification. By integrating BERT, our method demonstrates superior performance on the COVID19-BERT dataset, achieving 83.20% accuracy, 83.52% precision, 82.96% sensitivity, and 80.90% area under the curve. Moreover, ablation studies confirm that utilizing multiple sample volumes is pivotal to achieving high classification performance, and fine-tuning the BERT network with labeled data yields further improvements. Ultimately, our results confirm the effectiveness and reliability of the proposed classification framework. The framework has been incorporated into a diagnostic system that is currently in use at Guangdong Provincial People's Hospital. By automatically identifying COVID-19 cases, the system helps clinicians as it provides them with with classification results as well as detailed diagnostic features. Ultimately, the proposed framework may assist healthcare professionals in analyzing CT scans when available, and aid in data annotation when resources are limited. The study of eco-evolutionary dynamics is being limited by an exclusive focus on fast-changing ecology and evolution, typically occurring over short periods, as evidenced by the rapid changes observed in Trinidadian guppies and other laboratory and natural populations. We argue this perspective is overly narrow and neglects potential interactions on longer timescales.  We expand the scope of eco-evolutionary dynamics to incorporate slower evolutionary changes which span centuries to millennia.  For instance, feedback loops between changing landscapes and evolving plant life.  We also recognize that rates of ecological and evolutionary changes are influenced by modulators like temperature, thus allowing for synchronization or decoupling between these processes.  Notably, global climate change might amplify instances of eco-evolution and novel system behaviors, making it increasingly difficult to forecast these complex changes.  By adopting an integrated, interdisciplinary approach spanning from genetics to geomorphology and across varying timescales, we strive to improve our understanding of the complex interactions within eco-evolutionary systems.  This expanded perspective, particularly considering the influence of slow-changing environmental factors, may produce unexpected outcomes under global change, thus providing an essential framework for predicting future system behaviors in various contexts.  Ultimately, incorporating insights from both fast-evolving and slow-changing systems may allow for a more accurate and nuanced forecasting capability.  We use examples from diverse contexts such as changes in landscapes created by erosion and deposition, alterations to coastal ecosystems, modifications to marine ecosystems, and adjustments to human populations, to illustrate how incorporating slower-changing feedback loops can improve our forecasting ability.  By embracing this expanded perspective of eco-evolutionary dynamics, we may be better prepared to tackle the complex challenges posed by global change and mitigate potential uncertainties associated with these systems.  Ultimately, this could lead to a more effective conservation biology capabilities. Our research focuses on the underlying structure of Automated Market Makers (AMMs), 
a prevalent form of blockchain-based, decentralized exchanges. 
We reveal that the order processing mechanism results in token value diminishment for market liquidity suppliers under circumstances of heightened token price volatility. 
AMMs are adopted predominantly when their supported token combinations have significant use or price movements are strongly interconnected. 
However, the steeper pricing curve actually diminishes arbitrage challenges, though this benefits investors at a decreased rate. 
Conversely, the inclusion of numerous tokens worsens the arbitrage dilemma. 
We furnish empirical support for our primary model outcomes by using detailed transaction records of AMMs and AMF-based token price comparisons with SMS-based market prices from 2018. 
The outcomes of our study underscore the necessity for customized monetary policies tailored to the distinct characteristics of AMMs. 
AMMs are found to excel in markets requiring low token price stability or insignificant token price correlations. 
On the other hand, the suitability of AMMs is highlighted for markets characterized by token price volatility and interconnectivity. 
In such scenarios, the usual monitoring by regulatory authorities is insufficient; instead, the success of AMMs relies heavily on the interdependence of token price volatility. 
AMMs are unlikely to flourish in markets characterized by token price volatility and interconnectivity beyond a certain threshold. 
The relatively short lifespan of AMMs supporting token price volatility and interconnectivity below a certain threshold further underscores their limited adaptability. 
Customized monetary policies can either extend the duration of AMMs or ensure their sustained success. 
AMMs tend to experience increased adoption during periods of heightened token price volatility and interconnectivity. 
The pricing curve's curvature has a dual effect, namely a tougher arbitrage condition in terms of token price, but also a decreased rate of return for investors. 
The inclusion of additional tokens in the platform results in increased price volatility for market liquidity suppliers while also narrowing the platform's broader accessibility. 
We propose that Automated Market Makers should focus on token price volatility and interconnectivity when formulating their monetary and liquidity policies respectively. 
In general, the success of AMMs relies heavily on the interdependence of token price volatility.

A new analytical technique is proposed to assess how sensitive conclusions about important variables are to data gaps. This method utilizes a Bayesian framework combining multiple models, each built using a different imputation of missing data. Together, the models create a distribution on various parameter spaces. We examine how the uncertainty in these parameter estimates relates to the data gaps using a Bayesian version of a well-known statistical measure. We apply this analytical technique to data from weight loss trials, focusing on the relationship between reported food diary data and outcome results, for both fully and partially observed datasets. We also compare its results to alternative approaches such as multiple imputation and Bayesian net model analysis. The proposed method encompasses various Bayesian models, allowing for accurate Bayesian inference even with limited observed data. We conduct comprehensive simulations to evaluate its performance in terms of finding relevant relationships and reducing bias in estimating critical variables. The results indicate that this analytical technique achieves the desired trade-off between finding relevant relationships and minimizing bias. Furthermore, we analyze the data from a 15-month primary care-based behavior change program, investigating how baseline characteristics, self-motivation, and treatment influence weight and physical activity outcomes. The findings from this analysis highlight the weight loss treatment's efficacy, although the program did not have a notable long-term impact on participants' weights. However, we discovered a significant and positive correlation between program measures and multiple critical variables. These measures appeared to be unaffected by data gaps in program and multiple imputation data. The method also enabled us to create a predictive distribution for critical variables that are fully observed in program data. The results show that program measures consistently emerge as the best predictors across various data sets and multiple imputations. Nevertheless, its performance is limited by semantic inconsistencies between datasets. To optimize visual-textual alignment for CLIP models on various tasks, we introduce a technique that refines image-text cross-modality learning via VT-CLIP. VT-CLIP updates the cross-modal transformer's image and text encoder's linear projections in accordance with the current image-text pair distances during pre-training, thereby enhancing its robustness to diverse perturbations. Furthermore, we customize VT-CLIP for the backdoor attack to generate two types of systematic distortions: image tampering and text manipulation. The results demonstrate that VT-CLIP outperforms the original CLIP model in several benchmarks, including ImageNet and Cinematic Text. Our method also facilitates the creation of versatile and robust feature detectors for diverse perturbations. Source code is available at https://github.com/optimizingHL/VT-CLIP. Accurately predicting non-performing loans is a key factor for banks and other lending entities who need to balance taking on credit risks to achieve profitable growth.  There's a surge in interest from financial institutions to adopt advanced supervised learning methodologies for predicting loan defaults.  The proposed research is an illustration of a more general study on predicting credit risks, focusing on an actual credit dataset from the Brazilian banking system and making actionable observations from our analysis, especially regarding the importance of customer factors in evaluating risk, and highlighting the limitations of predicting loan defaults due to data limitations.  Notably, this paper contributes to existing research by conducting a comprehensive evaluation of classification models for predicting credit risks, and offers practical advice for banks and financial institutions looking to adopt machine-learning based solutions for facing challenges associated with data scarcity.  The paper's main objective is to share our experience and considerations when working in this domain, and offer valuable resources for researchers and professionals working in this field to facilitate reproducibility.  The results of our analysis show that, despite using sophisticated models with multiple parameters, the best possible accuracy we could achieve was just under 87\%, which is primarily due to data constraints rather than model performance.  In light of these findings, we draw three important conclusions: first, the success of our results is largely due to the properties of our dataset; second, when working with small datasets, transfer learning can be a useful strategy; and third, while time-related features are crucial, they are not enough to overcome data limitations.  In conclusion, while sophisticated models can decrease the gap between predicted and actual labels, they cannot overcome fundamental obstacles presented by data with only 17 relevant features.  In light of these unique challenges, adopting specialized techniques from the fields of feature selection and domain selection may contribute to addressing this issue, which in turn could improve the performance of the models by addressing this issue. Deep learning models, specifically Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs), are capable of generating robust image representations, but are limited when dealing with orientation transformations. To address this limitation, we have developed a novel model, Orientation Convolution Networks (OCNs), based on Landmark Gabor Filters (LGFs), which can learn, matching image patterns regardless of their orientation. LGFs, utilizing hand-designed Gabor filters with predefined landmarks, allow the OCNs to focus on the most significant image features. This distinguishes OCNs from traditional neural architectures. Furthermore, LGFs can be seamlessly integrated with existing DCNNs through parameter-sharing, making it a viable solution for improving low-level image processing. To test the performance of our OCNs, we have conducted a comprehensive evaluation on a range of datasets, including some with orientation variability and other complex image classification challenges, demonstrating its effectiveness in extracting robust, orientation-neutral features. Compared to OCNs, DCNNs require an additional step to rotate their feature maps into a standardized orientation, but our results show that OCNs outperform conventional networks in image recognition tasks. To promote reproducibility, the source code for our novel OCNs model has been made publicly available on both GitHub and SageMaker. This software enables researchers to reproduce our experiments, develop new techniques, and apply our OCNs model across various applications. Moreover, we have also released a custom dataset, named Dataset-O, comprising images from popular benchmarking datasets (e.g., CIFAR10/100, Tiny-ImageNet, EMQU, PubMed, NCI) with predefined landmarks, which can be used to replicate our findings and validate new methods. To facilitate cross-platform usage of our novel OCNs model, we have also provided a accompanying SageMaker recipe, allowing researchers to run experiments on local machines, Amazon's SageMaker, or other cloud platforms like Google Colab and Google Kubernetes. By sharing our work in an entirely open-source manner, we aspire to accelerate research in image recognition and expand the applications of deep learning models. Specifically, this means obtaining a localized version of the trace formula equivalent to the nine-term identity, generalizing the work of Chen. Furthermore, this approach enables us to prove an explicit version of the fundamental lemma for spherical double relative trace formulas. By merging this result with Wang's recipe and Guerati--Rennema's work, we are able to validate the Ginzburg--Rallis--Zagier conjecture for specific instances of the Simon's relative trace formula, encompassing special cases of the Deligne--Racine conjecture and pressing for its general applicability. The framework established in this research is versatile and can be utilized to validate distinct conjectures, such as pressing cases of the Burungale--He--Qiu conjecture and pressing cases of the Tzanaki conjecture, all via identical techniques. word definitions, although conventional dictionaries may struggle with 
capturing word meanings that vary across specific contexts. A potential solution 
is introduced in this study: the LitMind Dictionary, an online dictionary platform 
accessible through a web interface. It can automatically produce a definition 
based on user-provided words and surrounding context. Furthermore, the LitMind 
Dictionary supports multilingual queries, enabling the generation of definitions 
for Chinese and English, as well as cross-language inquiries between these two 
languages. A simplified user interface enables quick comprehension of query 
syntax and enhances the overall user experience. The LitMind Dictionary is 
available for public use at https://litmind.github.io. Both the dictionary and 
its source code are accessible on GitHub under the repository litmind/litmind. 

This research outlines the mind dictionary's key innovations and evaluates its 
output quality, demonstrating its advantages over prior work and highlighting 
areas for further improvement. Finally, a user evaluation is conducted to assess 
the dictionary's usability and user satisfaction levels. The results indicate that 
the mind dictionary outperforms its competitors in both output quality and user 
experience.

significant enhancements, specifically supporting multilingual queries and

41 languages. A publicly accessible interface for accessing the mind dictionary

Recent studies have exposed limitations in local surrogate-based post-hoc explanations regarding their inherent reliability, especially in critical applications such as human-centric recommendation tasks. Moreover, an ideal explanation should enhance key aspects of user experience including clarity and trustworthiness, posing additional challenges to the current approaches. However, a classical post-hoc model utilizing regression for explanation has inherent drawbacks including the lack of guarantee in effectiveness and the reliance on complex models which can lead to dependencies on highly complex and hard-to-understand models when attempting to simplify explanations. Moreover, an ideal explanation should not only accurately capture item-level preferences but also generalize well to unobserved items, necessitating a reevaluation of the current paradigm and techniques in this context. using semiconductor materials with unique electron properties from nanoscale
quantum wells made of InAs and Fe. Research on InAs quantum wells with a thin layer
of Fe shows that surface texture in significant to electron mobility and
conductivity. Upon annealing the samples at 150 degrees Celsius, the surface
morphology improves, leading to enhanced electron performance. Notably, when in the
presence of air, Fe intermixes and broadens during this process but its electron
properties remain the same. Investigaing the annealing effects on InAs quantum wells
with varying levels of Fe thickness reveals that any observable improvements in
electron mobility are limited, yet when the thickness of Fe is 2 monolayers or more
and the wells are capped with 5 nanometers of InAs, the results demonstrate
certain advantages. These improved performance when compared to standard samples
without prior annealing may be due to reduced disorder from monolayer variations
in the wells. Ultimately, electron mobility and conductivity of these InAs quantum
wells can be improved with proper surface texture which is achieved through the
annealing process. These findings highlight an alternative method to enhance
quantum devices based on superconducting properties that are compatible with
existing Fe-based superconducting technology. Furthermore, these InAs quantum wells
with unique electron properties may also find applications in other areas such as
cosmic rays detection, highly sensitive magnetometers, and more.

The study of how chronic diseases evolve throughout an individual's lifetime has primarily been based on an environmental perspective. This perspective considers early life experiences and later lifestyle behaviors as interacting and influencing future health paths. Inspired by the examination of social life patterns, which are known as social trajectories, we propose a similar analytical approach for medical studies. This methodological innovation combines multiple data sources, including administrative records and in-depth reports, to trace health changes. The technique is initially tested with an analysis of the development of obesity, which examined whether specific markers indicating health risks or medical issues, as well as reports from a physician or hospital visits, serve as critical signs of future obesity diagnoses. The study found that medical interactions with a child's healthcare providers significantly increase the likelihood of their future obesity diagnosis. The research also demonstrates that medical histories since a child's birth and future obesity diagnoses appear to occur in patterns, specifically clustering at specific time periods. These findings have implications for how we understand the progression of chronic diseases and the effective timing of preventive interventions. Furthermore, they highlight the value of examining longitudinal patterns in medical data, which may reveal valuable insights not apparent in standard static analyses. The technique of tracing health patterns could be applied to various fields, including social studies, with potential extensions to multiple data sources and diverse research questions. The study's methodology and code have been openly shared, providing a framework for future researchers to follow. One widely accepted method for evaluating electronic integrals in complex molecules involves a modified version of the original partitioning scheme designed by Christoph Leininger and Martin Head-Gordon, drawing upon work by Frank Neese and Simon Lennartsson. This original scheme sought to replace the straightforward but computationally expensive method used by Jack Hermans by utilizing a more efficient multiplicative partitioning of the Fock matrix. A notable improvement was introduced by Michael Frateau and Xavier Gao, who analyzed the error contribution of different regions in the partitioning and proposed a weighted sum that achieved a substantial reduction in computational cost while maintaining accuracy. Our work aims to build upon the success of this improvement by applying a similar approach to evaluate quadruple excitations within the resolution-of-the-identity coupled-cluster theory. Similar to the improved Leininger-HdG scheme, this method evaluates four-index ERIs by projecting them onto diagonal blocks of the AO Fock matrix, but with three key differences. Firstly, we use CI vectors from CCSD instead of RPA states, as they provide a more accurate description of the virtual space. Past and potential future Earth climate states have included extremely warm 'hothouse' environments with unknown atmospheric behavior, characterized by a distinctive low atmospheric heating pattern. In contrast to typical cooling effects, 'hothouse' climates are distinguished by a blocked window region for water vapor, which has led to theories of resulting temperature inversions and altered cloud formations. Prior climate modeling has failed to resolve turbulent air motions and cloud dynamics directly, leaving significant gaps in understanding hothouse climate processes. In this research, simulations resolving convection explicitly found that 'hothouse' low atmospheric heating shifts the water cycle from steady state to a periodic regime, characterized by intense precipitation and long dry spells. The time-averaged distribution of precipitation was similar to non-hothouse climates; however, 'hothouse' climates lacked a distinct tropical radiation gap and instead displayed dry patterns. The critical threshold for this periodic behavior was found to be a low atmospheric heating rate of 1.5 K/day, albeit speculative, and this finding supports the notion that 'hothouse' climates are characterized by a missing radiation gap. The exact physical mechanism behind this behavior was unclear but it was noted that periodic behavior was influenced by the interplay between local convection patterns and large-scale atmospheric dynamics. In a total functions logic such as HOL, certain non-terminating functions are difficult to define directly.  We introduce "clocks" to facilitate the creation of well-defined, non-termining functions in HOL.  A clock can monitor the progress of a function, triggering termination when the observer deems it appropriate.  This clock mechanism enables us to prove statements about non-terminating functions and their relationship to terminating functions.  We use this feature to formalize a version of the Russell paradox.  Additionally, clock theory provides a useful tool for analyzing functions with an unbounded domain or range.  This includes the translation of some real numbers, left and right infinity, and other extended values.  Clocks also allow us to validate an iterative method for approximating left infinity, originally described by Donald Knuth.  We incorporate these developments within the HOL light library.  Ultimately, this clock theory enables us to construct a map from the Baire space of natural numbers to the set of real numbers with an infinite decimal expansion, mirroring a well-known result by John Harrison.  This contribution is substantial in that it constitutes an entire new logic for handling extended mathematical objects.  Although clock theory can be applied broadly, in this context we focus primarily on the purpose of ultimately using it to define the real numbers.  A comprehensive overview of this theory is presented in the accompanying technical report, while the core developments are highlighted in a series of introductory documents.  This work makes use of the contrib tool for automated management of contributions to increase flexibility in the development and testing process.  Contrib facilitates the creation and testing of inferences and generalizes existing HOL constructs in line with the spirit of Euclid's five postulates.  Although contrib is not necessary for operating clock theory through interactive proof, it simplifies the process of translating algorithms to HOL and enhances the flexibility of the system by allowing pre-defined procedures for tasks such as finding a particular numeric value that satisfies a given criterion.  Ultimately, as an application of contrib's "interface" component, this work also investigates how to effectively integrate with the contrib module browser for searching and accessing available algorithms in HOL.  This study makes use of contrib's features for defining and importing both logic and computational functions in HOL.  As an example of handling complex data structures, we examine how to effectively utilize clock theory to define and manipulate various types, including graphs with an infinite number of nodes, regular expressions, regular sets, lists of unbounded length, and maps with an infinite number of key-value pairs.

A crucial aspect of theoretical models for screening involves the presence of a well-defined reference state, to which screening elements react in order to release tension.  However, amorphous materials, lacking such a reference point, still demonstrate screening effects resulting from plastic events which have a considerable influence on the mechanical behavior of the material. This discovery highlights hexagonal boron nitride as an efficient supporter for silicene's electronic transitions. Smoothed particle hydrodynamics possesses innate conservation capabilities, which remain flawless when accurately integrated, maintaining machine-precise levels of total mass, energy, and linear/angular momentum conservation. Notably, this property holds significant value in computational astrophysics for processes such as binary interactions and compact object mergers. Although the inclusion of gravity in such applications leads to excessive computation in pairwise interactions, a Fast Multipole Method variant addresses this by substituting interactions between distant particle clusters, which however introduces inaccuracies in angular momentum conservation. Our modification of this algorithm eradicates spurious torques, guaranteeing angular momentum conservation without substantial computational overhead compared to standard FMM. In simulated post-merger dynamics, our implementation confirms the preservation of angular momentum conservation not only in the knowledge level but also in the real-world particle dynamics. Our results show that even small residual torque inaccuracies can lead to early spinline alignment and second-time axis change. Ultimately, this accelerates the coalescence of disks surrounding rotating black holes compared to implementations without robust angular momentum conservation. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/Tobias-Prangenberg/FMM-sph-pc. A thorough, user-friendly benchmark including SPH timings and visual results are provided. Instead of relying on step-by-step instructions for implementation, a pre-made version of the SPH code is offered to facilitate seamless integration into existing toolboxes and engines. Our benchmark includes CPU-based Solar-mass body calculations in three-dimensional space, alongside a holistic performance analysis in both CPU and GPU environments. Furthermore, for researchers working primarily with GPUs, our implementation in the HOCBP environment offers an easily adaptable and efficient solution, which is accompanied by a basic benchmark demonstrating its compatibility and performance. A comprehensive, theoretical explanation of the SPH method and its potential shortcomings in massive fluid dynamics simulations are provided, alongside currently available approaches to rectify these issues and future avenues for research explored. In cases where a comprehensive, openly available solution is unavailable, a basic prototype of the SPH method is provided in the appendix, alongside a detailed, theoretical explanation of the random particle movement strategy. A modified version of this random movement protocol is currently employed in the SPH code used throughout this work. We develop a novel, yet efficient, method for augmenting existing data to enhance the learning capacity of reinforcement and imitation learning from experienced models. The policy cloning approach, a fundamental component of various learning techniques, is our focus, as it's the foundation for several off-policy deep reinforcement learning methods. To overcome the limitation of these methods, we designed PSOoC, a method that determines optimal actions by resolving a constrained optimization problem to produce imaginary transitions that complement existing data. We showcase PSOoC's performance in both offline and partial online settings, demonstrating its ability to learn optimal policies with reduced requirements for user-generated samples, especially for tasks that are easy to model and difficult to learn from experiences. We further observed that, in addition to its efficiency, PSOoC is suitable for zero-shot imitation off-policy without needing to train the target model using the provided demonstrations. Comprehensive experiments were conducted to validate the advantages of PSOoC in both the two settings mentioned above. Atomic magnetometers that utilize self-oscillating technology and driven by resonant modulation demonstrate enhanced sensitivity and dynamic range capabilities.
This technology, in conjunction with phase-coherent feedback from detected signals to modulation, enables the creation of a resonant spin maser system highly sensitive to changes in background magnetic fields.
Our system incorporates digital signal processing integrated into the maser feedback loop, realigns the phase in real-time, and employs a radio frequency based algorithm to identify spectral resonances.
The adapted technique also corrects for frequency fluctuations resulting from secondary detected non-resonant effects produced by precessing atomic spins in inhomogeneous magnetic fields.
Using this self-oscillating maser approach, we have successfully detected and analyzed the dynamic changes in background magnetic fields with a maximum detectable change of $1\mathrm{fT/s}$ within a $10\mathrm{Hz}$ bandwidth.
Furthermore, we have also demonstrated the ability to provide a mobile, geographically localized magnetic field map with a precision of $50\mathrm{mG}$ by applying the self-oscillating maser technique in various locations. All testing was conducted in a setting with a background magnetic field strength of $0.03\mathrm{mG}$.
Our research explores the potential applications of a self-oscillating maser system, highlighting its usefulness in detecting magnetic field changes within portable devices and its application in detecting nitroxide EPR signals from biological samples. 
Future enhancements to our system could involve the use of a high-order phase detector to improve its resistance to noise and minimize data loss when detecting resonant frequency shifts, enabling the detection of magnetic field changes at rates as high as $100\mathrm{Hz}$.
By implementing advanced algorithms such as the ones used in analyzing industrial resonant coils, our system can detect and analyze background magnetic field changes at very fast rates.
Our system has also demonstrated resistance to noise and intrinsic system inaccuracies, enabling our technique to work effectively in the presence of a $0.03\mathrm{G}$ background magnetic field - nearly 100,000 times more potent than our detected changes. 
Our system has also demonstrated practical applications by providing precise readings of magnetic field changes within portable devices and overcoming noise and system inaccuracies to do so. 
We also found that our system has sufficient resolution to detect and analyze nitroxide EPR signals derived from biological samples, making our technology useful in analyzing samples used in various medical and biological applications.

Our approach to training a neural network to identify hate-speech in Hindi and Bengali is outlined in this work. We investigate the viability of leveraging transfer learning for these languages, which lack sufficient labeled datasets, by using a pre-trained multilingual model and integrating domain-specific data into it. To achieve this, we create two new datasets comprising comments from different social media platforms in Hindi and Bengali that have been manually annotated for hate-speech. These datasets are then utilized to refine the multilingual model's capabilities for the #HatsofNewYork and SMM7 tasks. Furthermore, we explore the impact of distinct language variants, namely, formal and informal, on the performance of hate-speech detection models. Through our experiments, we determine that combining pre-trained models with domain-specific data leads to the best results and that using hate-speech datasets from other languages is not as effective as we had hypothesized. The findings also reveal that using informal language datasets offers greater benefits than using formal language datasets for hate-speech detection in Hindi and Bengali. Given the scarcity of labelled data in these languages, our approach offers an efficient solution. To facilitate future research, we will be making our code and datasets available for public use. The new datasets can be found at https://github.com/multimodalAI/HateSpeechHC/tree/main/hatespeech_data, while the code can be accessed at https://github.com/multimodalAI/HateSpeechHC/tree/main/code. In nuclear and particle physics, being able to identify the direction of nuclear recoils is a significant advantage. This capability, achievable at low energies, could help verify that a signal originates from particles with mass, over a background produced by neutrinos, by reconstructing the trajectory of those particles. This is particularly important for dark matter research and neutrino investigations. Since detecting recoils with angles of just a few degrees is challenging, the development of appropriate readout techniques is necessary. We have developed and tested such a method using liquid xenon detectors, involving analyzing and analyzing the electric field's influence on ionization electrons. This technique, dubbed Directional Analysis of Ionization Time, is demonstrated in a small LXe time-projection chamber with a gas gap. Our study shows that it's possible to determine the direction of nuclear recoils with margins of approximately 68% for energies of 10 keV. The competition highlighted an underinvestigated area in Optical Character Recognition (OCR) technology: accurately reading previously unseen text in real-world images during model training.
The dataset compiled for the competition comprises a diverse collection of 326,385 images, encompassing 4,864,405 text instances.
To address the challenge, a distinct validation and test set was created, comprising scene text that was not present in the training data.
The competition featured two recognition tasks: a holistic approach to reading full text and a focused task involving cropped text segments.
The analysis of baseline models and those submitted by competitors revealed a significant disparity between their performance levels in the newly introduced setting.
The proposed dataset will play a crucial role in further research to enhance the development of more versatile scene text recognition models that can adapt to unprecedented scene text instances.

Despite its high accuracy, ASK has a computational disadvantage in dealing with multi-dimensional systems due to the complexity of its integrations. To address this limitation, we have developed a sparse-grid-based ASK method (SG-ASK) that significantly reduces the computational burden. By replacing integrations with a traditional method on a sparse grid while maintaining spectral accuracy through polynomial approximation, SG-ASK achieves a substantial speedup. Experimental results demonstrate that SG-ASK is able to achieve a significant cost-performance tradeoff while maintaining high accuracy in approximating the dominant dynamics of multi-dimensional systems. Furthermore, SG-ASK offers an adaptable implementation that can be tailored to various problem-specific requirements. Notably, we have successfully applied SG-ASK to two challenging real-world applications, namely modeling biochemical reaction networks and predicting chaotic dynamics in a waterwheel system. The assessment of SG-ASK's accuracy revealed that it can effectively approximate multi-dimensional system dynamics with high precision even when the number of spatial dimensions reaches several times the number of poles in the spectral approximation. Notably, the error can be further minimized by increasing the number of poles while maintaining a reasonable level of spatial dimensionality. The Sinkhorn algorithm remains a widely-used solution to the Schrödinger problem. While it's well-documented that this algorithm converges when a solution exists, a linear convergence rate is achieved only if both the solution and the reference coupling have the same support. Considering that structured stochastic processes may result in degenerate scenarios where the solution does not exist, research demonstrates that even in such situations, the Sinkhorn algorithm leads to two specific points of convergence. Crucially, these limit points enable the calculation of a solution to a more relaxed version of the original problem. The relaxed version can be thought of as the result of replacing the original problem's marginal constraints with marginal penalizations in a related problem. As a result of these findings, a new theoretical framework has been established that allows for the determination of the solution support in both the original and the relaxed problem for any reference coupling and marginal constraints. We demonstrate the potential effectiveness of this theoretical framework through a promising application in a cell biology model. Given that the Sinkhorn algorithm's macroscopic behavior mirrors its convergent points, these findings also contribute to a deeper understanding of the Sinkhorn balance and its extensions to multi-marginal problems. Consequently, these results may facilitate the development of novel structures in both Euclidean and discrete contexts. Lastly, the properties of the Sinkhorn algorithm in relation to specific structured stochastic processes have been explored, resulting in the identification of scenarios where the Sinkhorn algorithm's convergence can be guaranteed. While this guarantee is linked to the solution's existence, a linear convergence rate is only assured when the solution is reached after the algorithm has completed an infinite number of iterations. Notably, this result holds even when the algorithm is only run for a finite number of steps. As these results demonstrate, the properties of the Sinkhorn algorithm are not only relevant at a theoretical level but also have significant practical implications for its safe and effective use in a variety of domains. While this framework focuses on the Sinkhorn algorithm, its generalization to other structured stochastic algorithms is possible and is currently being explored. In probabilistic learning, organisms sometimes opt for a less than optimal strategy known as probability-matching, which means choosing options based on their reward probabilities, as opposed to the optimal strategy, maximization, which involves consistently selecting the option with the highest reward.  Despite years of study, the factors leading to probability-matching are still unclear and an interesting aspect is the similarity between this and maximization behaviors when observed in organisms such as zebrafish, which offer a valuable simple system to study this issue.  Using a new version of the standard decision-making model from Bush and Gold (2004) that we modified, we found that we could recreate the probability-matching strategy with a high degree of accuracy by assuming that there was some uncertainty about the true reward probabilities.  By testing our model with various levels of uncertainty and different lengths of the decision-making process, we were able to verify its effectiveness in explaining the probability-matching phenomenon, including cases where probability-matching breaks down when the uncertainty is too great.  Our model also predicted an observed (Bush and Azulay, 2018) transition from probability-matching to maximization at relatively low levels of uncertainty, which matches our experimental results from choosing different colors in a Markov decision process for the zebrafish reward.  By assuming that the brain has access to some degree of uncertainty about a given decision-making process, our model offers an interesting new way of understanding the probability-matching phenomenon that offers a clear vision of how organisms can learn and evolve through decision-making processes.  By testing our model, we were also able to verify its effectiveness in explaining other decision-making phenomena, including case studies of probability-matching on both a local and global level as well as global maximization, which includes scenarios of interim analysis in decision-making processes.  By utilizing an Atkins symmetric star graph for our analysis, we were also able to verify our model's effectiveness through a high degree of accuracy in explaining a wide range of different industrial and biological decision-making phenomena that we tested, including cases where probability-matching breaks down in favor of maximization.  By looking at the distributional six sided die assumption (i.e. probability-matching) vs. a precise number-based distribution (i.e. maximization), we were also able to verify our model's effectiveness in offering a clear choice between these two options based on the level of uncertainty, which means that our model offers a clear understanding of how uncertainty impacts the probability-matching vs. maximization debate in decision-making processes. To mitigate systematic measurement errors on quantum computers, current methods employ counteractive postprocessing techniques known as measurement error mitigation (MEM). A key limitation of these techniques is the tradeoff between scalability and validity: methods that handle a large number of qubits tend to produce negative probabilities, whereas those that guarantee a correct probability distribution cannot be scaled. To address these concerns, we propose a new scheme that combines both principles. Specifically, we adapt and implement a standard iterative Bayesian unfolding approach commonly used in high-energy physics experiments in a way that scales effectively with the number of qubits. Our approach is validated by successfully mitigating measurement errors in experiments involving up to 127 qubits and 26 qubits using Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger and Bernstein-Vazirani algorithms, respectively. Notably, in the case of BHZ experiments, the Mott-tonality of retrieved qubit states can be nearly perfect, with probabilities exceeding 99% in the range of valid outcomes. These breakthroughs mark the first successful mitigation of measurement errors in experiments of such magnitude and complexity. Moreover, our findings highlight the potential of adapting and leveraging existing solutions from other fields to address the growing scalability and validity challenges in NISQ-era NISQ devices. When humans operate robot arms, it is frequently necessary for the robot to infer the task the human is attempting to accomplish. Current research on assistive teleoperation and shared control focuses on developing methods for the robot to determine the desired task based on human joystick inputs. Typically, this is done by using an internal map that links joystick inputs to specific tasks: for instance, pressing the joystick to the left indicates the desire to move a plate, while pressing it to the right signifies a cup. While this method works well after the user has grasped the robot's input interpretation, inexperienced users are required to discover these linkages through trial and error. We identify that the robot's input-task mapping is a standard procedure that can be executed in various ways to better inform users. By taking a proactive approach, the robot can establish an understanding of its own control conventions by teaching the internal map while the user performs a series of tasks using visual feedback. This can be achieved by framing the problem as an learning inverse multi-objective optimization problem. We further investigate the conditions under which the robot's input-task map will be uniform, or in other words, where the robot can learn a single task corresponding to a specific joystick input. Finally, we evaluate our concept in a study with 8 users who were presented with the standard trial-and-error procedure or our robot-controlled learning strategy. The results indicate that the robot's learning approach leads to fewer input interpretation mistakes and greater end-user satisfaction. The code related to this concept has been made available online. We believe that our method represents an essential advancement in assistive teleoperation and shared control, as it enhances both the overall operator experience and task efficiency. This knowledge has the potential to contribute to the development of more autonomous and autonomous robots that operate without human intervention. For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings independently, having an effective mapping system is crucial. Current mapping approaches rely heavily on state estimation techniques that minimize drifting and produce a unified global map for navigation. Unfortunately, implementing these systems on a large scale can be challenging due to their tendency to deviate and slow build-up times. In response to these limitations, a novel map representation called HiTMap is presented, featuring a unique hierarchical structure that focuses solely on representation, thus minimizing drifting and scale management. This system enables local maps to be detected and managed automatically, removing the need for manually configuring parameters to achieve a seamless representation. HiTMap's performance was successfully tested in various real-world scenarios, including indoor and outdoor environments with both small and large-scale features, achieving a local representation that accurately captures the environment and its scale. The results demonstrate HiTMap's capability to overcome the limitations of conventional mapping methods, providing a reliable representation for local navigation. A publicly accessible software implementation of HiTMap is available online for further research purposes. The authors' long-term goal is to combine the representation capabilities of HiTMap with state-of-the-art state estimation techniques to develop an optimized mapping system for large-scale environments. Research into two-dimensional arrays with favorable two-dimensional correlation properties has gained significant interest due to the rapid advancements in modern wireless communication technologies. Various applications of two-dimensional arrays can be found in areas such as ultra-wide band, millimeter wave communication, and 3D imaging. This paper presents a new method for constructing generalized quadrature amplitude modulation based two-dimensional arrays, referred to as the QAM two-dimensional array. The proposed two-dimensional array can be used in transmitter-side data preprocessing, offering benefits in anti-noise and anti-interference capabilities. A key advantage of the proposed two-dimensional array is its simplicity in construction, utilizing a single two-dimensional complex phase shifters set. Simulations of the proposed two-dimensional arrays have been conducted, highlighting their ability to robustly handle channel estimation in scenarios with limited training data. The performance of the proposed two-dimensional arrays has been evaluated using parameters such as bit error rate, normalized mean square error, and spectral efficiency. The results confirm the effectiveness of the proposed two-dimensional arrays in terms of link reliability and robustness in comparison to traditional carrier-based approaches. A comparison of the proposed two-dimensional arrays has been presented, using the parameter spectral efficiency, to showcase their superior performance in terms of link reliability and robustness. A two-dimensional sparse array was also explored, showcasing its ability to significantly improve channel estimation in scenarios with limited training data. A numerical example has been provided to illustrate the proposed two-dimensional sparse array, highlighting its potential in various applications. The research outcomes serve as a foundation for the development of two-dimensional communication technologies. A possible future direction of the research is suggested. Lastly, the relevant patents related to two-dimensional communication technologies have been introduced.

The comparison highlights an issue with divergence of local response models, where fields become infinite at boundaries between material regions. The impact of these effects on propagating electron fields, particularly at low frequencies, is significant and can potentially be observed through electron microscopy. The electron spillover effect propagates fields into material regions and connects fields at material boundaries, demonstrating that our systematic approach provides a unified understanding of electron behavior governed by both local and nonlocal electron behavior, which is essential for studying electron optics and the propagation phenomenon. The analysis also indicates that nonlocal behavior tends to suppress electron propagation into material regions compared to the local response model. The proposed systematic approach can be applied to various electron optics problems at low frequencies. The study provides insights into how local and nonlocal electron behavior can be used to explain a range of electron optics phenomena, which is crucial for understanding observations made using electron microscopes. In the era of vast information, search engines are indispensable tools that 
allow users to access specific content among numerous results. Most existing 
research on search engines has concentrated on the technical aspects, 
focusing on issues like text retrieval, ranking, and expansion. However, this 
paper takes a distinct approach, delving into the fundamental challenge of how 
users can engage more effectively in search tasks by participating in 
information retrieval. A key area of investigation involves the user's role in 
specifying terms with contextual significance, either drawing from their 
general knowledge or relying on external sources like dictionaries. To 
facilitate user involvement, a novel search system was designed to test the 
effects of human input in search tasks. Users were presented with three 
options: contributing their own context-bearing terms, selecting them from a 
pre-defined list, or accessing a web dictionary for possible terms. The system 
allowed users to either include all input context terms in the query or have them 
implicitly rank them for better results. A notable outcome of the experiment 
was that human involvement yielded superior outcomes, whether users provided 
one or multiple context-bearing terms. Furthermore, users who relied on their 
own knowledge or dictionaries outperformed those who used pre-ranked context 
bearings. A close examination of the results revealed several key insights. 
Firstly, users who contributed their own context-bearing terms or consulted 
dictionaries demonstrated superior retrieval performance. Secondly, while 
manual and automated methods of user involvement sometimes produced similar 
outcomes, those relying on user input were marked by reduced system dependency 
and greater satisfaction levels. Overall, this research highlights the 
significant role of user participation in search engines and suggests that 
encouraging user input in context-bearing terms can lead to enhanced 
information retrieval. The system designed for this study may serve as a 
prototype for future search engines, allowing them to effectively harness 
user input in query formation and evaluate the effects of various involvement 
strategies. The findings of this study also underscore the importance of 
tailoring system design to accommodate the capabilities and preferences of 
searchers, thereby fostering more effective user engagement. Finally, they 
stimulate crucial debates about the optimal strategies for enhancing user 
involvement in search engines and the potential consequences of different 
design choices on various groups of users. The research underlying this

Time-based data sets that correlate over time are common across various fields.
Such data frequently exhibits temporal dependencies, periodic patterns, and
variations in trend over time. Despite the underutilization of this type of
data, current machine learning techniques have not been sufficiently explored for
solving problems involving time series data. To fill this knowledge gap, an
online Microelectronic Laboratory educational platform was utilized for teaching
Machine Learning fundamentals through a series of time series-based exercises.
Here, we detail the creation of this platform. Each platform has three main
sections: an introduction with theoretical background and resources, an exercise
section featuring algorithmic tasks, and a visual section displaying results.
All content, including source code, scalables, and platform, can be found at
https://github.com/ptrio/gitsl. The scalables folder contains pre-set up
environments for solving problems in different programming languages. The
platform utilizes GITS.Lab's virtual collaborative environment and is hosted
on GitHub for knowledge sharing. The content scope is broad, encompassing
problems from different domains, such as multivariate data analysis, one-dimensional
time series analysis, and multi-dimensional plot generation. Each task includes
a description of the problem in natural language, a list of required library
dependencies, and a sample solution provided as feedback. The visual section
displays a summary of the exercised problems and their corresponding results.
The content creation process involved three stages. First, the platform was
populated with basic time series data such as means, medians, and random data.

variables with varying noise levels, and finally, tasks were designed for
complex data analysis, spanning two-dimensional regression, multivariate
analysis, and multi-dimensional plot generation. The platform offers time
series-based educational content, expanding the existing machine learning
curriculum and enhancing students' understanding of this underutilized form of
