The Turan number for an r-uniform graph F, denoted by ex(n, F), is defined as the maximum number of edges in an F-free r-uniform graph on n vertices. The Turan density of F, denoted by pi(F), is defined as the limit of the maximum number of edges over the total possible number of edges as the number of vertices approaches infinity. Erdos-Stone-Simonovits' theorem established that the set of possible Turan densities for 2-uniform graphs is infinite, and for 3-uniform graphs, irrational Turan densities have been discovered, disproving a previous conjecture. We investigate whether irrational Turan densities exist in certain cases and show that the Lagrangian density of a specific 3-uniform graph is sqrt(3)/3, resulting in an irrational Turan density, which answers an open question posed by Baber and Talbot. Furthermore, we generalize this result by determining the Turan density spectrum for graphs obtained by combining two complete graphs with an edge in an r-uniform setting. We also prove that lower bound estimates we established for these densities are in fact tight. The techniques used involve applications of the basic consistency proof, a generalized version of Bragdon's consistency proof, and Holshouser-Schensted's correspondence. We also utilize an integral linear form of Poljak and Tuza that bounds the maximum number of edges in an F-free r-uniform graph, and this approach yields sharpness when the graph is either a triangle or a triangle with two isolated vertices. We observe that this method may be applied to determine the maximum number of edges in an F-free r-uniform graph for specific cases where F has a maximum neighborhood size of two. We also propose a method for calculating the Turan number for large and rare graphs. We conclude by offering a general theory or framework for the so-called'structured extremal graph classification problem.' The efficiency of deep learning semantic segmentation algorithms in identifying abnormalities on chest X-rays is limited by the laborious task of gathering and annotating training data. To alleviate this issue, we explore how image enhancement techniques can lower the necessity for labelled data in chest X-ray pneumonia detection through semantic segmentation. By training UNet-style models on subsets of fully annotated images and assessing their performance using unbiased metrics from a separate, poorly annotated pool, we evaluate the effectiveness of seven image enhancement methods with varying levels of impact. Ultimately, the combination of rotation augmentation and random grey level scaling outperforms all other techniques, reducing required labelled data by 65% on average, making it the premier choice for minimizing data labelling needs. Moreover, we discovered that simply augmenting the labelled data, without retraining the model, yields a substantial 59% decrease in labelled data needed for optimal results. These findings not only help segmented object detection but also contribute significantly to the development of more efficient and self-sufficient image classification models. The research code is available at https://github.com/grasp-lyrl/image_segmentation_with_augmentation. The dataset used in this study can be accessed at https://figshare.com/articles/100k_images_for_chest_x_ray_pneumonia_detection/12219133. The work has been accepted for presentation at CBMS 2021. As autonomous systems become increasingly prevalent, it is essential to establish a legal and regulatory framework for addressing harm caused by these systems to individuals and properties. Failing to do so may result in a legal and law-abrief chaos. This research aims to clarify harm caused by autonomous systems by comparing existing definitions of harm in existing laws with a conceptual framework based on causal models. This framework incorporates the cause-specification principle, which is useful for explaining various types of accidents. Examples of how this framework can explain harm have been presented. Additionally, this study outlines the prerequisites for autonomous system policymakers and suggests a method for these policymakers to participate in normative specification processes, ultimately informing public policies. Finally, this research identifies challenges in implementing causal harm definitions in existing laws, particularly in contexts where accountability and moral causality are relevant. By focusing on causal models, this study demonstrates how three-dimensional models of reality can be used to identify causes for accidents, regardless of whether an accident occurs during routine, expected operations or unexpected variations. This causes-specification characteristic enables policymakers to develop causal-action plans that can prevent similar events from occurring in the future. Comparing the concept of harm in existing laws with a framework based on causal models has revealed that most laws focus solely on external observable consequences, such as property damage. Only a few laws, such as those in torts, consider the mental and emotional distress caused to individuals as part of harm. In contrast, the concept of harm in artificial intelligence, while varying depending on application, generally focuses on the external effects that autonomous systems produce. This research has identified a notable difference between explaining accidents caused by autonomous systems and accounting for the credit or blame associated with their causes. While causal models can explain accidents by identifying their causes, accounting for credit or blame requires considering not only causal models but also factors like intent, accountability and moral causality. Implementing causal harm definitions in existing laws is challenging because of the complex interplay between causality, intent and accountability. As shown in the empirical analysis, this implementation may face obstacles like cognitive biases that affect how people perceive causes for accidents. When policymakers do not participate in normative specification processes, this can lead to various problems, such as unanticipated consequences, shared credit or blame and the like, which are often referred to as "law-ills". Several options for addressing these challenges are discussed, including developing causal-action plans that consider the credit or blame associated with causing accidents, incorporating causal models into existing laws and establishing policies that promote causal-awareness among the public. Speech-to-text translation involves converting spoken language into written language across different tongues. Conventional two-stage approaches using speech recognition and machine translation have inherent flaws. An alternative method called zero-shot translation is gaining attention, where a single model attempts to translate between languages unencumbered by labeled data. However, current best practices in natural language processing are often at odds with each other when applied to zero-shot translation, such as usingocr models with larger vocabularies than the machine translator or combining multiple architectures with distinct training objectives. We investigate these trade-offs to determine their relative importance for zero-shot translation and the most effective methodologies to accomplish it. Furthermore, we explore the potential benefits of incorporating audio and task-specific information into the translation process. Our research is presented in a structured manner with each section building on the findings of previous sections, a approach commonly referred to as the WAKI strategy, where data augmentation, self-supervised, and instance-weighting strategies are combined to optimize results. The proposed solutions achieved exceptional front-end results across several languages and scenarios, achieving scores of 5-14% better than state-of-the-art baselines in key metrics. The code and model parameters for these solutions have been made publicly available. We believe our research offers valuable insights, a systematic approach to addressing challenges in zero-shot translation, and could potentially inform similar applications in image-to-text translation. A total of eight front-end configurations were tested on materials exploring multiple languages and domains, with the specifics outlined in Table 1, Table 2, and Table 3 in the paper. These experiments demonstrated the WAKI strategies yielded superior results to the best alternative methods. The analysis further identified instances where existing models were flawed and could be improved, such as a failure to effectively utilize audio inputs. The WAKI strategies proved particularly beneficial in challenging scenarios, such as when fewer examples than languages were available for training or when the translation request contained ungrammaticical or out-of-vocabulary words. The results further suggested that the complexity and parameter count of the models could be reduced without compromising results. The proposed methods, however, did not outperform pre-trained cross-language speech-to-text models in certain easy-domain scenarios. The models developed during these experiments, however, did show comparable performance to the best existing models when evaluated using standard metrics. This work introduces a novel extension of the traditional heat conduction theory, encompassing cases with fading memory and incorporating the standard heat equation under dynamic boundary conditions as a particular instance. We delve into the well-posedness of systems comprised of equations akin to those by Coleman and Gurtin, further subject to dynamic boundary conditions with memory. These systems contain nonlinear elements situated both internally and on the boundary, with their behavior either dictated by classical dissipation principles or governed by a nonlinear balance condition. Moreover, we allow for disparate memory kernels involved: uniformly convex in the internal space and uniformly monotone on the boundary. Consequently, this system encompasses a broad spectrum of problems: from classical wave dynamics in narrow filaments to models for biological tissues with temperature-dependent boundaries, all featuring uniformly convex boundary temperatures. By employing the Galerkin method for regularized problems and using the framework of two-time scale geometric dynamical systems in the case of memory, we prove the existence and stability of solutions for these systems. Notably, the presented approach holds significant promise for addressing many other physical problems, including dynamics in continuum media. Further research aims to explore its applicability to contact dynamics at interfaces. The resulting theoretical findings are complemented by numerical examples, with a primary focus on the internal fractional heat equation under dynamic boundary conditions. Furthermore, we include a comparative analysis with classical heat conduction theory and fractional heat conduction models. The presented work represents a significant advancement in the development of mathematical models for continuum dynamics, laying the groundwork for potential applications in various fields. A subsequent publication will investigate the existence of periodic and quasi-periodic solutions in boundary value problems. As an application, we will examine the one-dimensional case of the bio-heat transfer function for cancer treatment hyperthermia. Additionally, the final part of the series will be devoted to the existence of solutions for boundary value problems, including contact dynamics. Herein, we provide several numerical examples to demonstrate and illustrate the obtained results. Moreover, we validate the findings by comparing the proposed models with real-world data, highlighting their practical applications and emphasizing their potential to develop innovative technologies. In the final stage of the series, we will explore the existence of periodic solutions for boundary value problems, including cooling of large bodies, bio-heat transfer, and contact dynamics at interfaces. By leveraging the established framework, we demonstrate that the presented models possess a broad range of applicability, making them suitable for realistic physical and engineering scenarios. Precise short-term forecasts of energy consumption are essential for managing low voltage electricity networks efficiently, particularly with regard to highly disaggregated load distributions among a small number of customers, where individual behaviors tend to dominate aggregate consumption profiles. Since peak demand often drives energy distribution challenges, developing accurate timing and level predictions of daily peak demand is crucial, as traditional forecasting methods frequently struggle to characterize these spikes adequately. This issue highlights the need for an alternative forecasting technique that can better capture these daily peak demand events, ultimately improving the efficiency of energy-distributed networks. This study proposes a solution by integrating statistical time series modeling with the capabilities of grounded reality augmented gravity models, which incorporates commutability factors to account for routine activities influencing customer energy consumption during the workweek and weekends. By combining these features, the proposed model can capture both weekly and daily seasonal patterns effectively, leading to an improved estimation of time-varying parameters in energy consumption. This new method also addresses the problem of a shrinking population in networks by groundedly accounting for the routine activities of decreasing populations, which may include factors such as an aging population or large-scale industrial closures. This study conducts a comprehensive test of the new forecasting method using real-time energy consumption data from low voltage networks in the UK, comparing its performance to existing top methods such as Vector Autoregression, LSTMs, and GRU networks. The results demonstrate the superiority of the proposed model in predicting peak demand and daily/peak peaks, ultimately leading to reduced power outages in low voltage networks. Based on this outcome, the potential applications of the new method are discussed, including its potential to inform renewable energy integration, energy management for retrofits, and network thermal load assessments. Nonetheless, the proposed model does not entirely account for the highly stochastic nature of energy behavior at the level of individual detail, which is crucial for advanced distributed energy management systems and network planning. This limitation highlights the need for further research in this area to advance energy forecasting efficiency. The proposed method and associated data and implementation are open-source and accessible through GitHub, specifically at the following repository: https://github.com/c-krishnan/GroundedREGR. This initiative aims to foster collaboration and improve energy forecasting accuracy, ultimately advancing the field of energy research. Furthermore, the paper makes several recommendations for future research, including addressing the challenge of highly stochastic energy behavior at the level of individual detail, facilitating advanced distributed energy management and network planning. The new method is presented at the European Energy Forum, bringing together leading researchers and practitioners in the field to facilitate collaboration and knowledge-sharing

Accurate vertebrae localization and identification are crucial in various medical applications related to spine disorder diagnosis and surgical planning. However, certain pathological variations (e.g., vertebral compression fractures, scoliosis, vertebral fixation) and imaging conditions (e.g., metal artifacts in CT images) complicate automated classification tasks. To address these challenges, a new research study focuses on developing several classification techniques to accurately map three-dimensional vertebrae anatomy in CT images, especially in cases with vertebral body metal fixation. To achieve this goal, a dataset was created with anatomically segmented vertebral bodies containing various pathologies and imaging conditions. Several 3D CNN architecture-based classification methods were then proposed to address the complex classification tasks. When tested using the newly developed dataset, the study's results demonstrated improved accuracy in mapping vertebrae localization and identification in CT images with various pathologies and imaging conditions. One of the techniques, a multi-task CNN architecture, showed over 98% accuracy in both classification tasks and vertebrae CTV prediction. To further verify the study's findings, a comparison was conducted with existing literature, demonstrating that the proposed methods achieved better performance than previously reported results. One significant advantage of the study's methods is their potential for real-world clinical applications due to their simple and lightweight nature, requiring only about 60 parameters. To facilitate the advancement of spinal disease research, the study's results and dataset are made publicly available for further research purposes. A link to access the dataset can be found at https://github.com/CatalaoG/Vertebral_Recognition. A local copy of the dataset can also be obtained by contacting the study's corresponding author. Several online resources, including an online API for anatomical segmentation and classification, can be found at http://imav.usp.br/dormans/vertebral.html. In addition, a competition related to this study's findings can be found at https://www.geeksnecker.github.io/2021/. The study's results are presented in English. A Portuguese version of this study can be obtained by contacting the authors. To the best of the authors' knowledge, this study's results are the first to address automatic classification tasks in CT images containing metal fixation. A significant challenge to this study was identifying publicly available images with vertebrae metal fixation for training purposes. Our theory explores the behavior of electron collisions with a strong repulsive barrier in a contained environment. Within an extremely high level of electron interaction with the surrounding electromagnetic field, temporary variations in the field energy lead to a steady state formation of an entwined state confined at the center of the barrier. As an incoming electron's energy aligns with that of this confined state, it undergoes rapid, inelastic collision resulting in emission of a cavity-generated photon. We diverge from conventional methods of developing optimal controllers through in-depth modeling and simulation, instead directly teaching model-free controllers to the actual robot. Initially, gaits are generated through central pattern generators, whose parameters are fine-tuned to maximize energy efficiency by experimenting with different controller settings. This strategy is effectively demonstrated on a 1-meter tall five-link robot, showcasing the potential to rapidly produce viable controllers, even for complex systems. Furthermore, the adaptable nature of our approach enables it to successfully execute a diverse set of gaits, such as those adapted for different loads, accelerated velocities and tight turns. The evidence presented here reinforces that biologically inspired methods can produce optimal controllers, saving considerable design time and human expertise. The source code for the development process has been made publicly available. We intend to expand on this research by exploring the potential for humans to reconfigure the parameters of the CPGs through operant conditioning, mimicking reward-based training methods. We successfully tested this operationally conditioned CPG on the actual robot and observed the effects on its dynamics and resulting gaits. Ultimately, integrations like these could ultimately permit robots to autonomously adjust their locomotion strategies in response to their own dynamics, rather than pre-designed presets. We propose a new variational quantum algorithm, the Variational Separability Verifier (VSV), to identify the closest separable state of an arbitrary quantum state with minimal deviation in Hilbert-Schmidt distance. Our algorithm's performance is initially tested with GHZ states composed of up to seven qubits via numerical simulations. We also use VSV to generate certificates of strong separability for certain mixed states derived from two-qubit Maxwell-Boltzmann distributions, leveraging the property that states with zero correlation matrices are separable and maximally mixed. Furthermore, we apply VSV to find the closest separable state of a two-qubit state with arbitrary purity and examine the corresponding entanglement measures, including the entanglement of formation and the concurrence. Our results indicate that the performance of VSV significantly improves as the number of qubits in the GHZ state increases. Since VSV executes the same unitary transformation $U^\dag$ that's used in the implementation of quantum teleportation, it can be considered as an extension of the quantum teleportation algorithm. Our findings suggest that the proposed algorithm is computationally viable, even for larger numbers of qubits, as the depth of the circuit only grows linearly with the number of qubits. Moreover, the operations within each layer have stable resource requirements, such as quadratic qubits, linearly many single-qubit gates, and a single two-qubit gate, with the exception of specific scenarios where the two-qubit gate is absent when q is even. Our approach can be further enhanced by applying it to identify the closest separable states of multi-partite pure states with complex structures. With advancements in large-scale quantum computing hardware and the development of efficient variational algorithms, the proposed algorithm has the potential to reach higher levels of computational performance and facilitate the efficient treatment of quantum states with increasing numbers of qubits. As such, the proposed algorithm is scalable for use in near-term quantum computing applications. Moreover, the proposed algorithm can efficiently achieve the efficient treatment of states with increasing numbers of qubits, achieving computational efficiency while avoiding unnecessary numerical simulations that are prevalent in near-term quantum computing applications. Our approach can be applied to various applications, such as solving linear problems in quantum chemistry with near-term quantum machines, exploiting near-term quantum machines for graph classification in chemistry, and realizing quantum teleportation, among others. Since our algorithm, VSV, is versatile and can be used with different types of input states, such as pure or mixed states, provided they can be implemented on the quantum machine.

A surge in demand for search by image has led researchers to investigate fashion instance-level image retrieval, which involves finding matching images. Building upon this, the concept of fashion attribute manipulation, which modifies a specific attribute while retaining others, has emerged. This enables users to search not only identical items but also similar items with specific attributes. However, this task is challenging due to the need to accurately preserve the remaining attributes. In order to tackle this, we have developed a novel method based on style transfer techniques that allow for independent manipulation of attributes in fashion images. Our model is trained using real-world images and can efficiently apply both attributes from a given image and create desired attributes based on user specifications. Through experiments on a large, publicly available dataset, we have achieved state-of-the-art results in retrieving similar images and outperformed other methods in manipulating attributes in image search tasks. Additionally, we have confirmed our model's effectiveness in preserving the remaining attributes by conducting reidentification experiments on the manipulated images. The code and dataset can be accessed at https://github.com/Ankittw/FAMpy. Furthermore, we have highlighted our model's potential in explaining clothing items' attributes through a novel task where we have demonstrated our model's ability to fill missing attributes in clothing images. The accuracy of our model in this task has surpassed other methods, showcasing its explanatory capabilities. This demonstrates that our method not only manipulates attributes but can also interpret attributes in image search. Experimental results obtained from testing our model on two publicly available fashion image search datasets, including DeepFashion and OIFT, have validated the explanatory capabilities of our method. As a result, when a user asks for information on a specific trait in an image, our model can provide an answer while retaining the desired attributes. For example, if a user wants to know whether a yellow shirt is silk or not, our model can provide a yes or no answer while retaining the yellow and silk attributes. The outputs obtained from these experiments have validated the real-world applicability of our model in explaining attributes in image search. In the future, we plan to investigate more categories of attributes for a broader explanation capability. Additionally, we have identified a few limitations in our model's current implementation, such as the need to balance the competition between attribute manipulation and image reidentification. Through our experiments, we have confirmed our model's reidentification capabilities are on par with other methods. However, there is room for improvement in having our method reap apply attribute manipulation to reidentification tasks. This area of investigation shall be explored in the future. Lastly

The $\R$-optimal solution for the underdetermined equation $Ax=y$ where $A$ is a bounded linear operator mapping a Banach space to a Hilbert space, and $\R$ is a strongly convex function defined in that space, is considered for cases of incomplete data and noisy input. A dual gradient approach, though suffering from semi-convergence, can approximate the sought-after solution. Due to its underdetermined nature, the method requires an optimal stopping time, for which three rules – a priori choice, the discrepancy principle, and dynamic thresholding – are considered along with respective convergence results established. Convergence speeds for these are compared under specific conditions such as the existence of a minimum, a weakly convex function, and various regularity of the desired solution being discussed along with several numerical experiments that validate these findings. Constructing the matching cost is a time-consuming step in estimating light field depth. Many previous studies first converted depth maps into blurring kernels and then convolved LEAs to generate the matching cost. The underlying kernels, however, are often difficult to interpret, causing existing methods to rely on heuristic search. A faster cost constructor, which converts depth maps into binary occlusion labels and directly combines with RGB colors, is proposed in this study. These binary labels can be generated by an unsupervised neural network trained by a highly correlated, yet much simpler benchmark. The cost constructor's simplicity and speed enable it to be integrated into a neural network for light field depth estimation as a differentiable function. A large dataset, RF-100, is also used to train the network. The results show that this method outperforms state-of-the-art methods, particularly in noisy and highly variable light fields. A decreased estimation time of two orders of magnitude is observed as well. Furthermore, this study introduces the concept of sub-aperture angle modulation to improve estimation accuracy for extremely turbulent light fields. A higher density of sub-aperture angles can efficiently capture the occlusion geometry, but increases estimation time. By integrating this concept with the novel cost constructor, even the weakest GPUs can facilitate accurate 6NLF depth estimation, opening new avenues for practical applications. This study uses the bilinear method to investigate the Fokas-Lenells equations, first reducing the system and then employing double Wronskian solutions to yield a range of solutions for the reduced equations, resulting in a comprehensive overview of solutions for both classical and nonlocal Fokas-Lenells equations. Several solutions are illustrated through asymptotic analysis, notably double line soliton solutions and superposition of two circular wave solutions, which contradict prior theories of two superposed circular wave solutions for this system.  Moreover, by using the four-field Lax pair for the FL equation, we obtain two pairs of mirror solutions of level-crossing and level-repelling solitations, one of which has been previously documented.  All solutions to the FL equation, whether classical or nonlocal, can be derived using bilinear equations, yielding support for the idea that the FL equation is completely integrable.  Finally, this investigation confirms recent observations that the FL equation does not admit linear wave solutions, which were initially suspected through numerical analysis.  All results for the FL equation were implemented using fourier kernel software to enhance the accuracy of these results.  Fourier kernel, a novel open source MATLAB tool, was developed or this investigation.  Moreover, fourier kernel provides a general framework for testing integrability of nonlinear evolution equations by checking compatibility of fourier series expansions with their respective bilinear forms.  As such, fourier kernel is particularly suited for testing integrability of equations featuring periodic or localized data, such as soliton-type solutions, which are notoriously difficult to analyze using Fourier transforms.  A comprehensive user manual is provided for fourier kernel, which is available for open access at https://github.com/ZJJe/Fourier-Kernel.  Furthermore, the code utilized  in this investigation has been posted at https://github.com/ZJJe/Fokas-Lenells-EL. Alternative theories of gravity that go beyond the Riemannian framework have been proposed to explore quantum gravity and model systems with non-relativistic symmetry. However, developing these theories involves a complex task: deriving an action principle that accurately captures their behavior. This technical note utilizes the double field theory formalism to establish action frameworks for these alternative gravity theories, thereby simplifying this challenging task. By doing so, it resolves issues related to previously constructed actions that lacked integrity and integrity violations. Furthermore, this note explores the Torsion bilinears that emerge from these new actions, demonstrating their potential to tune non-hierarchical states of these alternative gravity theories. Finally, it outlines a potential application of this framework to modeling condensates of torsion that appear in double field theory. By tuning the torsion condensation, it is possible to recover existing actions of gravity theory. This reveals an unexplored area of research: investigating how torsion impacts existing gravity theory models with relativistic symmetry. This, in turn, may pave the way for modeling materials with torsion that are composed of non-hierarchical states, such as, for example, ultra-cold atoms.
